translations.text: 1. [?] But not less than was fitting. Brief exchanges were able to acquire [?] such power.
And to encounter in my mind, in an undying way, the perfect love of your chastity. For even if I take refuge in another wisdom,
which is acquired after involvement in practical affairs, nevertheless, immediately and through that very goodness of your perfect love, may I find abundant delight,
when the fruits of careful examination are yielded at the proper time, through the abundant showers of God’s grace.
And may the gloom of the air change from the winter of troubles to the brightness of spring, and may light dawn upon us in salvation from the great Sun of Righteousness.
Then our mouth will be filled with laughter and our tongue with praise. And then they will say among the nations,
“The Lord has done great things for these people.” And we too will say in response, “The Lord has done great things for us, and we have become joyful.”
To him be glory forever. Amen. Why, then, wise man, have you grown weary of asking after the welfare of your friends
with a few lines on paper? For apparently you are not pleased even when they write to you. For I, since I once became bound to the love of your honored person,
and I consider it an excellent good [?] to you, it pleases you. For I, since I once became bound to the love of your honored person,
and I consider the exchange of reminders of you an excellent good, through such commerce in letters,
have now resolved to meet you in person. And I do not think that you will reject the eagerness of my mind.
If, then, you wish to receive these words gladly, do not withhold the good gift of your thoughts from those who are waiting to receive news of your health.
Greet your companion in your labors. All the holy ones here greet you, those who have not grown weary of praying for us
at the offering of the holy mysteries. And may [?] fulfill—at the offering of the holy mysteries. And may God fulfill their petition concerning you through the mercies of his grace. Amen.
2. To the community of monks, concerning zeal for the faith.

To our father, holy in every respect, the blessed Mar Babai: give your blessing. Ishoʿyahb: greetings in our Lord. If the practice of goodness, our father, were distinguished in every generation by the honor it deserves,
the world would consequently have been easy even for those who engage with feeble strength in the struggle of battle.
For praise from the many would have given additional strength to the weakness of their zeal, and encouragements of this kind
would have increased their boldness in speaking on behalf of truth. And the triumph of victory would have belonged to truth alone,
and not to its servants. But now, when every danger from enemies outside is already accompanied by grumbling from those within,
and, third, along with these comes the weakness of the human mind in the hardship of the times that have brought general distress,
together also with the evil of disobedience that has taken hold of many, and the apostle’s declaration has already received
its due fulfillment—“In the last times,” he says, “people will be lovers of themselves,” and the rest of the passage—and the multitude of other things that were foretold through the Holy Spirit
many generations ago are now being fulfilled in practice by the children of disobedience, the progress of our faith is shown through these things [?] to be difficult to sustain.
What song of praise is not his due—he who, amid waves of despair, steers the ship of faith with the rudders of his preaching,
and fills his city with abundant nourishment from the trade in spiritual life?
For in the face of such danger from savage storms, with the ardor of your zeal overcoming the length of your years, O our father, holy in every way,
you have been able to show that all the satanic schemes of bodily demons are powerless.
For it seems right to me to call the wicked by this name. Even the ruler of the air, although at his creation he received an excellent nature from the good Creator,
nevertheless earned this name for himself through wickedness against God. Consequently, those who inherit his dominion also inevitably seize for themselves the inheritance of his name.
Such chief demons, then, enemies of [?], and the [?], unyielding partners in their wickedness,
together with all the violence of their madness, were easily burned up by the fire of your divine zeal. And as the radiance of its flame consumed the wickedness of their insolence like stubble,
it made the way of truth free from stumbling for those who delighted in enjoying the light of the gospel of Christ’s glory.
Amid the assaults of enemies, the grumbling of those within, and all the distress of the time, the glory of your zeal shines triumphantly with praise from God.
May he, in his goodness, exalt your honor through his grace, to console his faithful people for many years. Amen.
3. To a certain physician, concerning news of illness.
To our honored, God-loving brother Mar Sergius: Ishoyahb sends greetings in our Lord. Our common nature, brother, in those equal in the strength of their [?],
makes the very same foods act through the enjoyment of nourishment,
either by transformation and increase to promote the growth and maintenance of the body, or by producing the tormenting pains that occur.
Thus, amid such customary afflictions, the souls of all of us are likewise subjected to the harsh nourishment of adverse reports, which torment us with misfortune.
How, or from what necessity, did it happen that I, together with everyone here who loves you, should be compelled to suffer great grief on receiving news of your [?] and of those you love?
The matter has dragged on excessively for us, since no further good news countering the bad was quickly brought to us.

Take care, then, brother, and remember to let us know now how the protecting care of God’s grace is treating you. You will bring great joy to our goodwill toward you, which longs to hear good news about you,
so that, filled with consolation at your relief, we may join you at every moment in giving thanks for God’s mercy toward you. May he in his grace always preserve you from every harm. Amen.
4. To a great and renowned solitary, concerning the grievous events that occurred against the faith.
To our father, holy in every way, Mar Hnanisho: your son Ishoyahb sends greetings in our Lord. For the mystery of lawlessness, our father, has already begun to stir.
Amid the violence of the pressing labor pains, the birth of evil is expected. Now, I think, is the time for correction to take effect in everything.
For look at the darkness of the many afflictions that the time has brought upon us, and the famine of the good things that sustain human life:
the root of Christianity has begun to dry up in the heat caused by the lack of priests who keep the branches of the beloved plant flourishing.
And the destruction that remained in the village among the rest of the negligent; and, besides all these things, the departure from bodily life of that leader who loved the faith.

As soon as she went out, there was also the arrival of that Magian, the persecutor of the fear of God, together with the grief of many who had lost even the hope of living without the danger of suffering.
These became an ominous sign to many discerning people. And the rest of the other events, which strengthen the discerning people's indications of a common disaster,
proclaim clearly enough, as I said, the mystery of lawlessness and the revelation of the lawless one.
But more distressing to discerning people than anything else is the sleep of negligence that has overcome the guardians of the truth. What, then, remains for weak people like me,
by which they might gain a little consolation, except this thing that I have now wished to do: to send you, a leader who loves God, the sounds of my sighing in a letter,
so that, by stirring your fatherly compassion through the recollection of our common disaster, I may soon find a pledge
of consolation through the visitation of God's grace, by the petition of your prayer, and the eyes of the blind may see out of darkness and gloom.
For good labor for the salvation of everyone is especially fitting for your fatherly love of God.
Through it, from the height of your years, you have reached a glorious completion in which you may triumph. So, in concluding with a hand that offers no help,
may the remembrance of my weakness not depart from your fatherly prayer, so that perhaps I may be found worthy to spend the rest of my days in a life pleasing to God's will.
5. To the teacher of Erbil, because he had asked after him by name in a letter to the head of the monastery, and concerning his care for the imprisoned confessors.
To Mar Daniel, excellent in every way, teacher of [?]: Ishoʿyahb sends greetings in our Lord. When, with conscious understanding, I proudly received the homage of your humility, modest one,
it seemed to me a way of nourishing your noble desire to respond both individually and collectively, with greater fellowship, to those things through which you honored me.
For when I encountered your greeting addressed to us in common, I felt great joy at the nature of your gift. The fear of showing contempt alarmed me if I did not reply,
but the danger of displaying my lack of learning frightened me if I did reply. There remained, then, a course between these two that seemed appropriate: to respond in a mixed manner,
so that in one respect I might appear as I actually am—that is, an unlearned man—and in another as I am thought to be,
namely, someone who flees vainglory. If, then, it is natural for waves to gather even without a deep sea,
and customary in writing for mounds of persuasion to rise toward the intended goal,
and the distribution of the stars in relation to light is a matter of necessity, and the whole course of change toward its cause is a providential arrangement,
so too the abundant birth within the mind of different kinds of thoughts, unrelated to one another, is customary [?] in rational discourse—as all these things are clearer to you than to anyone else.
How much less objectionable it is, then, if the poverty of my understanding ventures to mingle, through the openings of contemplation, with the deep and many-recessed ocean of your wise mind.
That mind, when it rose to the stature of that renowned theologian and mingled with the character of his eloquence, drank in as an heir [?] the impressions of his insights.
And in you, at all times, just as now, it has acted as a philosopher of spiritual things. And the order that had concealed customary practice
it shows to be more compassionate, skillfully adapting the sweetness of the rules to the accustomed taste, and filling the poverty of barren portions with an abundance of wisdom.
And [?] the common good, so that we may accomplish it—the common good that the thought, impulse, and care of individuals have brought about.
And this while he suffers, while he is spoken of as a dog, while he endures the repayment of injuries, while he labors to do good.
Rather, the children of God, while he cries out with the leader of the contests, if necessity presses, even to disown Christ, if possible [?].
In return for making many righteous, understand this—namely, you who in everything are an instrument of reason
and of the cultivation of spiritual seeds; and now also a minister of [?], and their pledge [?] for praise.
Rather, to Christ imprisoned, sick, hungry, thirsty, and naked—to you who, on behalf of everyone, share every day in blessed sufferings—with what shall I come forward to offer sacrifice
and repay a fruit worthy of the deed, of the blessedness that [?] in exchange for these things, or of the glory
that is concealed in pains, or of your humility toward us? Yet we cannot even add strength to your strength through our encouragement,
just as a star cannot benefit the sun. For, I think, nothing remains for us to ask on your behalf, except those things that belong to the Lord:
namely, the success of his purposes in you. May he himself, in his goodness, bring the whole labor of your good deeds to completion through the mercies of his grace. Amen.
6. To the same believer mentioned above, concerning his trial.
Ishoyahb to Sabroy, my brother in our Lord: greetings. “For now mercies have drawn nearer to us than when we believed,” says the blessed apostle.
For when we measure the severity of the affliction that has befallen us against the increase of the fruits that come from discipline, my dear friend,
let us proclaim this very [?] of the apostle, until it pleases their good God to grant a helpful outcome at the appropriate time.
For even the earth, the mother of all, when she receives into her body the pain of wounds from the dragging of the plowshare,
then offers useful fruits more abundantly. Know indeed, my dear friend, that we have spent most of our days in the indulgence of harmful things.
Like uncultivated ground, we have grown a forest of desires. But as for wheat, either we have rejected it altogether, or we have carelessly made it grow mixed with weeds.
For this reason, the providence of God’s mercies, cultivating our barrenness through measured trials, gathers joyful fruits for our benefit at the time of [?].
For we are certainly persuaded, as good disciples, by the apostle of God,
who cries out to us every day, saying, “Endure discipline, then, because God deals
with you as with children.” May he, in his goodness, [?] the visitation of his mercies for our salvation. Amen.
7. To his cellmate at the School of Nisibis.
Ishoyahb to Surmazd, my brother in our Lord: greetings. You have been very bold, modest man, and you have supplied powerful material for increasing my patience.

I therefore beg your modesty that someone as receptive as I am may be found to receive every insult from your wisdom. For perhaps in this way, as time passes, a remnant of those who love you will remain.
For while I gladly receive the bites of your childishness into the body of my thoughts, I persevere nobly, so that I may never be compelled to give up the exchange of [?].
to empty myself of the delight that refreshes the spirit [?], as I undertake to breathe into the openings [?] of your letter praises befitting your honor.
You surely do not doubt that this can happen if I wish. May God give you wisdom in everything and strengthen you to preserve the unity of love in the bond of [?].
8. To the abbot of the monastery of Mar Sliba, concerning the afflictions after the death of Yazrin.
To the servant of the Lord and worker of righteousness, Mar Sabrisho: Ishoʿyahb sends greetings in our Lord. For my part, as you know, holy man of God,
even in times past I could scarcely, and only after many days, satisfy my mind’s longing for beauty through [?] your presence. For it is fitting for providential care
that the memory of the holiness of someone whose virtue has already been demonstrated by experience before convincing perception should be preserved in inviolable treasuries.
For the excellent fulfillment of your will surpassed my earlier choice, and [?] I considered it also a fitting debt of love
that, through my own feeble ability, I should always repay your love with fitting expressions of goodwill.
So now too, as I entertain such thoughts and offer an expression of sympathy at a time [?], I am, as it were, nourishing myself with my meager understanding.
Therefore, virtuous man, courageously meet the force of the changes that time has brought you with the strength of endurance.
For it is neither possible nor attainable for anyone to sail through the troubled depths of this changing world without being shaken by distressing waves.
For you, more than anyone, have the revered ocean [?] and sign of salvation, which can keep the ship of your mind unshaken in the storm of this time.
For when it was once [?], it shook the earth and killed death; and from that time onward, every day, it casts down legions of demons when it is used in faith.
How much more will it distinguish you above everyone through daily deliverance, as a servant of its holiness,
so that, when you are kept free from all suffering, we too may be able to enjoy your company without disturbance.
And thanksgiving befitting such care will increase through the well-being of many, to the glory of Christ. May he, in his grace, preserve you from everything harmful. Amen.
9. To a friend, after the devastation by the Romans.
Ishoʿyahb to Sergius: greetings in our Lord. Because the storm of war has stirred up with its turmoil the sea
of the world, my beloved, and with the whirlwind of the waves of captivity has shaken the ships of humanity to every end of the inhabited earth,

and the remnant has been stranded on the reefs of fear alone, like the survivors in the days of Noah, the thought of loved ones is therefore in the torment of uncertainty, awaiting news of those who bring them joy.
From the confusion of reports, as though from the crest of the waves of the deep, we receive an impression of well-being.
But the flickering of our longing has not yet been stilled by reliable news. Therefore take care, virtuous man,
if you are still alive in the body, to gladden us with news of your well-being, either by coming or by a letter.
Perhaps, when you learn what has happened to us, you will lighten our burden by sharing in the work of consolation.

We, however, are like a firebrand from the fire, [?] our Lord, who shows us mercy in everything. At the same time, we also pray that we may soon welcome you in person with joy. May God preserve you from every evil. Amen.
7. To a monk, concerning the death of his master.
To our father, excellent in every way, the honored Mar Abdisho: Ishoyahb sends greetings in our Lord. That man of God who was able to receive a double portion of the spirit of prophecy,
when the fiery prophet was sent to heaven in a chariot of fire, mingled Israel’s bereavement with his own grief.
With a cry of lamentation he uttered words fitting his grief. Although he was very firmly assured of the promise concerning his request,
nevertheless, his faith was overcome by distress, and he contemplated the ranks of Israel according to the flesh, stripped of the armor of prophecy.
For this reason he also wailed. Indeed, in a situation resembling his, how can all of us who fear God not be compelled in every way to grieve,
when the chariot and horsemen of the spiritual Israel—that is, the commander of the forces of the church’s [?], the mighty tower of spiritual conduct,
the one who bore in a mortal body a pattern of the life after the resurrection, the hornet whose divine zeal continually consumed all the filth of evil teachings,
the one holy in everything and revered by everyone, the perfect image of virtue, our blessed father Mar Hnanisho [?]—
was sent away, at this time of greatest need, to the land rich in saints? For the pain of bereavement is powerful, and it penetrates the depths of our natural affections.
It acts with great force to kindle love for excellent things. Yet sometimes hope in the promises to come also rises above it.
But often it also struggles against [?] in faith itself. Thus it makes its pain keenly known through sufferings like these.
For this reason, in similar circumstances we must mingle something similar with our grief—we who have been left to endure the pains of separation from a spiritual father.

For although he did not anoint a second Elisha for us with a double portion of the strength of his zeal, but only with the brightness of his rays, this man is able to cover with the light of his truth
the darkness that presses upon us, and to settle without distress, in the tranquility of faith, those who persevere in the good inheritance of the holy [?].
And although such an anointing is still hidden from bodily perception, God is faithful in his promises, for the Lord does not abandon his people or forsake his inheritance.

Therefore it is necessary that, as we await from the lookout of the sons of the prophets the dividing of the Jordan, which helps bring the promises to fulfillment, we should then cast away from ourselves the fear caused by doubts,
and arm ourselves with the hope that confirms us, as with a coat of iron. At the proper time, let us display a confidence worthy of our boasting in our Lord.
And may the grace that abounds among many have its thanksgiving increased through many, to the glory of Christ. Amen.
As for me, holy man of God, the departure of that holy leader from bodily life at this time suddenly dealt me a wound.
I was still tormented by uncertainty in my thoughts, and withdrawal from everyone seemed to me useful for remedying my need.
Through constant changes of place, one’s awareness may be diverted from distressing [?]. Therefore I ask your holiness to pray.

Make an even greater effort so that the distress that has overtaken us may once again be swallowed up in our joy, and so that, through the flourishing of your virtues, the grounds for everyone’s boasting may increase.
Remember me too every day, so that through the petition of your prayer I may be found worthy of God’s mercies, and may soon also enjoy a joyful meeting with you in person.
Convey my heartfelt greetings, with your loving kiss, to the blessed fathers and the holy brothers who are with you. All the saints here send you greetings.
11. To the brothers on Mount Izla, concerning the death of their head.
To the servant of God, our holy father Mar Habib, together with the blessed fathers and holy brothers who labor with him in spiritual service:
Ishoyahb, a son embraced by the love of your fatherhood: greetings in our Lord. I never imagined, O holy men of God, that [?] before the onslaught of adversities.
I was destined to see the eagerness of my will brought low [?] in its pursuit of its noble desire, and in all this, so that not only
would I suffer through being deprived of your beneficial company, but I would also be emptied of all the consolation of the joyful hopes conveyed by a letter.
But the intensity of sorrow weighed still more heavily upon me because, on your side no less than on mine, the possibility of a visit had been taken away.
For I hope in our Lord that I will soon find everything set right in an encounter with your love, which is full of every consolation.
For the distressing troubles I have endured until now, both publicly and privately, will be left for lengthy conversations,
in which we shall enjoy the cheerfulness of one another’s faces with joy, with God’s help.
But since the evidence of daily adversities reproaches our weakness with failure in everything, turn your attention to me, I ask you,
and console me in my need with the good news of your well-being [?], and of how the providence of God’s grace is guiding your cheerful company,
after you sent the man of God to heaven and placed that head, exalted and illustrious in everything, among the ranks of the saints [?].
For who deserves more than you to glory in blessings, since you fill the kingdom of heaven with saints of the Most High?
These men, having taught people in the East [?] the orders of spiritual service in the manner of angels,
and having been raised from the fleshly world to incorruptible life, impressed upon you, as upon pure gold, the image of their way of life.
And the honored [?] image of the fear of God is the fruit of their diligence among you, the bearers [?] of their labors.
For among these and others like them, the foremost is that blessed man, holy in every way, our angelic [?] father Mar Babai.
Who among those who have once been renewed in the spirit of their minds, according to the apostle’s command, would not consider his wondrous [?] departure at the fitting [?] time worthy of blessings
and a legacy of praise for times to come? For even though there is mingled with joy
the agitation of bodily sorrow, since we always need the support of someone who shares our nature, nevertheless the evidence of what has happened lessens the violence of sorrow.
For it is within God’s power, as it is written, even from the dead among us to raise up in every generation living people who are fit to console his faithful ones.
I am also confident that the blessing of his grace will be firmly preserved among you to the end, as a demonstration of his love for his saints.
Remember, then, those days, day after day, in which you endured great struggles through sufferings for the truth,
and how you became a public spectacle [?] before those who corrupt the faith, and courageously endured their arrogance with joy.
And you did not allow the disguise of those in error to obscure the light of truth, even slightly in words.
Rather, in the openness of truth you have made the boldness of your good confession shine before everyone. Even the mouths of your enemies are compelled to proclaim the triumph of your testimony.
Thus you have these daily commemorations everywhere as witnesses to your steadfastness in the holy Church.
To preserve the truth of the faith through a worthy confession, and to excel in the practice of the spiritual way of life handed down by our holy fathers.
When you fulfill all these things [?] with God's help, as I confidently expect,
nothing will then be lacking for a good and perfect hope, nor will there be anything requiring prayer among the things that call for the exercise of one's strength.
Rather, everything, whenever it is remembered, makes me share in its joy. I pray only that such goodness may endure forever,
to the praise of our truth and the [?] of the upright. I ask your fatherly love to keep the memory of my weakness in your holy prayers,
so that perhaps I may be able to spend the rest of my days living in a way that pleases the will of my God.
12. To the brothers on Mount Izla, concerning the delay in answering and concerning an adverse report.
To the servants of God and diligent workers of virtue:
Our holy father, Mar Habib, together with the blessed fathers and holy brothers who together on Mount Izla, in the inheritance of our father Abraham, excel in spiritual ministry.
Ishoyahb, a son shared by your fatherly love: greetings in our Lord. I acknowledge, O holy men of God, that last year I wrote to your love, crying out in pain,
because the force of the obstacles had prevailed, pressing to cut off my eager desire to meet you in person.
At that time, that is, the suffering was shared, since for a long time we had been unable to meet one another even through letters from afar.
But from then until now, since I expressed my pain while you remained silent, the weight of suffering apparently continues to rest on me alone,
both because of my solitude and because of my longing, and perhaps also because of my excessive faintheartedness.
While I was thus waiting in the past for news of your affairs, O holy men of God, the storm of my sins swept me away to the abyss of Seleucia.
I have been compelled to remain there for a long time, right up to the present—not so much for any other reason as because of the law of love.
For the daily increase in those who love me kept adding to the length of my stay there,
especially as my work was advancing in the hope of benefit. But when it appeared, it greatly gladdened me [?].
13. To a monk who was called to lead another monastery.
Ishoyahb to Paul, my brother: greetings in our Lord. I heard about your coming, and I also read what you wrote to me. You did not do well to make your coming uncertain.
For this is not fitting for someone on whose spirit people always rely amid every pressing change.
But perhaps, because of the great simplicity of your character, you regard your move from place to place as instruction in manners, conduct, and reputation.
Do not think of it that way. Instead, take with you everywhere the [?] of a stranger and a humble mind.
And they will accompany you in all your affairs, and you will find rest. Always pour out your soul before our Lord, as indeed you already do.
And let your will always conform to God's will, so that he may guide you in all your affairs along the way of his truth.
Rely on the truth and fear nothing. For those who speak the truth can rebuke even the king of the land.
Especially if they also reveal the truth that they speak. As for the brothers who are with you, do not be their teacher as though teaching on your own authority.
Instead, simply remind them of our Lord's commandments and the teachings of the fathers. And when you have reminded them, urge them to observe them.
If they act blindly [?], judge them with love. If they argue, call them to witness concerning your departure. And if they urge you to remain,
urge them to keep the commandments. If they do not keep them, they have already made it known to you that you are not required to remain with them.
And if it is necessary to leave, set out plainly before them the reason for your departure. Leave without anger and without reproach,
leaving behind you no just accusation for reckless tongues to make. All these things, then, are for bearing with a lack of
willingness to be persuaded. But if they obey the beneficial commandments, the wealth of virtue is then not [?] shared by them and you.
Continue teaching, so that you may grow richer. Above everything else, take particular care to teach about love.
First give an example of it yourself, so that your words may be more readily accepted and the benefit to the community may increase. As for the longstanding customs of the place,
those that you may have to change, contend against them little by little. First persuade them of what is better, and then abolish what is inferior.
Thus, when the matters in question are judged by comparison with one another, the superiority of what you propose will become greater.
If they observe it, they will know that you have been a teacher of what is good to them. If they do not observe it, they will know that they have rejected what is good.
In short: remain where there is benefit, and leave where there is benefit. Count as benefit what your conscience bears witness to.
Do not let your mind rush into anything. Instead, bring everything into the court of your thoughts, and examine it justly in the fear of God.
Hold fast to what is good. May the God of peace himself give you peace in your dwelling and equip you with every good work to do his will,
so that you may be strengthened with every strength, according to the [?] of his will, to the glory of God himself and for our encouragement.
Pray also for me, that I may spend the rest of my days living in a way pleasing to God's will. Our brother Mar Hnanisho and the brothers with me send you greetings.
Give greetings to the brothers with you, and urge them to pray for my weakness.
14. To a certain teacher, concerning illness and poverty.
To the man of labors and diligent worker in true teaching, the chaste and God-loving Mar Hahai, priest and teacher: Ishoyahb sends greetings in our Lord.
I received and read your letter to me, O lover of God, which contained a great demonstration of how little love there was. And I thanked our Lord for your health.
For this is a sign of little love: to compose a hymn of praises with an abundance of persuasive words, and send our friends this demonstration of our attitude.
To write [?] or say such things to others out of sincere affection amounts, that is, to a small act of care.
But when we offer such things to the person himself, we do not altogether escape the dangers of flattery.
Therefore, O lover of God, the testimony of our mind is sufficient proof for us of the sincerity of our love. We also trust that, with God's help, it will remain unshaken forever.
I have heard, O lover of God, that the hand of robbers has brought severe poverty upon you. And I have also heard
that the illness that befell you has brought you great bodily weakness, and that because of these two things you are suffering distress of mind.
Such thinking, then, does not befit your years, O chaste one. In what respect do you suppose that he is now powerless, when you have seventy years of evidence of his care?
For anxiety over either of these things is a sickness for a soul that hopes in God, and all the more so for a teacher of the truth.
Through faintheartedness, then, as I suppose, you had clung to the possession of both these things. With impoverished hopes, you had placed your trust in bodily health
and in material possessions outside the body. For this reason the Spirit of the Lord blew upon both, so that your hope concerning both might turn back to the Lord.
Hope, then, in the Lord, as befits your understanding, and gladly endure the delight that comes from poverty and illnesses: in the one, as far as Lazarus,
and in the other, as far as Job, and in both, as far as the praise that comes from God. May he, in his providence, bring to completion
the honor of your old age in glorious fashion, through the good desire of your mind, to the glory of God himself and for our encouragement.
For I have begun to travel along the road that you know. Pray, then, that this journey may be directed according to our Lord's will, and that I may see you in peace, with joy from God.
15. An impassioned address to the Catholicos concerning the accusation over fleeing.
To our father, holy in every respect, the venerable Mar Ishoʿyahb, Catholicos and Patriarch. From Ishoʿyahb: peace in our Lord.
Sufficiently [?], I think, there has been set out in what I have already reported an account showing the distress of my mind over the events that occurred,
and why, contrary to the intended goal, the outcome was left uncertain. For it is clear to many that certain people had set a limit to the suffering before they compelled us.
But, as it seems to me, the force of that statement proved false in this affair. It brought about a change in what was expected, not merely at odds with the goal, but completely opposed to it.
For I took the many days that had passed as evidence of my endurance, and continued in hope until the pressure became acute.
And when I was compelled to leave, I left a written account of my affairs to be presented before your fatherhood,
and stated that I am remaining in this monastery as though in the courtyard of the church of Kokhe, waiting to hear gladly whatever God may command through the mouth of your holiness.
I openly made a fitting prostration at your feet to show the suffering of my mind. Take care, then, O chaste one,
that, while carrying out the work that befits you for the glory of God, you also restore me to life as a beloved son,
and grant abundant joy to all who fear God everywhere. For zeal on behalf of the truth is fitting [?] and proper for you more than for anyone else,
and many reasons [?] us, while the conscience of many is inflamed over them.
May the provider of our blessings cause the truth of his teaching to prosper through your hands, for the glory of all. Amen.
16. A greeting to yesterday’s friend.
To our father, honored in every way, the holy Mar Theodore, bishop: your son Ishoʿyahb sends greetings in our Lord.
If the sovereign will that longs for what is good were successful in every matter, our father, nothing would prevent
my satisfying the longing of my mind, before any other undertaking, through an encounter with your fatherly love. For I long for this both because of my position and because of my disposition.
Because of my position, on account of the commitment previously made by letter, through which, in the beauty of adoption, you made me a member of your fatherly household.
And because of my disposition, on account of the cheerful delight of those very patterns of thought,
through which, in a single agreement of mind, we praise the one truth common to all and are diligent sons of the very same good inheritance of the blessed fathers.
For this reason, fellowship of this kind is praiseworthy in the eyes of the wise. Because of it, I long to hurry to meet you in person.
For although the adversities that arose have temporarily prevented my coming there, I hope in our Lord that I will come soon.
My hope will succeed if I receive the necessary help from the petition of prayer. But I am delaying a few days
until I visit the scattered people of Assyria outside this enclosure where I am.
I acknowledge that I deserve to be afflicted with such a lot, for in the past I did nothing worthy of the grace
of God toward me. For this reason I now reap the fruit of my negligence in daily turmoil. But thanks be to God, who directs everything for our help.
Pray, I beg you, that I may spend the remainder of my days in a life pleasing to the will of God.
17. To the brothers in the monastery of Izla who were harassed by their brothers and suffered harm from them.
To the chaste brothers on Mount Izla, who strive in spiritual service within the inheritance of our father Abraham, lovers of God and workers of virtue, my lords and brothers:
Habib, Dazuzai, Gregory, Luke, Arzisho, Stephen, Yazdin, Barduq, Simeon, and the chaste brothers with them.
Ishoʿyahb, your brother, sends greetings in our Lord. Through an abundance of deceptive hope, I have apparently suffered the burden of years, O mighty men,
because I had raised my confidence in you above every fear. I never expected that, subdued by the adversities that arise,
I would see you as you are now, since through many demonstrations you had gained practice in not being defeated by trials,
such as Satan, the common enemy, habitually brings about. But now, after I wrote to you twice and you remained silent without replying,
we perceived, that is, the evil that was to be expected—the very thing that I have now heard has befallen you to suffer.
For this reason, as I wail in pain, I use expressions such as these:
Who, then, broke down the protective fence of that lovely vineyard, which was flourishing with the fruits of righteousness, and made it a trampling ground for every foot?
The impurities of the wicked. Who was it, then, who shook that mighty tower, fortified on every side, as if by secret tunneling, and brought the arrogance of its strength down to the ground?
Who was it, then, who did this to the ranks of spiritual warriors, those who had so often carried off a true victory against the onslaught of human rulers?
Now, amid peace within the household, they have produced division within it. And, as though with a sharp sword, he has removed the leading commanders from their appointed ranks.
Who was it, then, who entered the strong man's courtyard, found him stripped of his armor, and seized his possessions? To put it more plainly:
Who was it, then, who took the beloved [?] of righteous Abraham, the good heirs of righteous Dadisho, and the chaste disciples of victorious Babai—
those for whom everything was one and held in common: faith and conduct, soul and speech, and every good practice—
and has now miserably forced them to suffer [?] from one another? But it is clear that an enemy has done this: the evil demon who hates humanity.
He is the one who long ago sowed the seed of disobedience in paradise and afterward brought forth a new murderer in the plain.
In every generation, through evil servants, he has brought grievous destruction upon our nature.
Even now he is no less arrogant: he has fallen upon you amid what seemed to be peace pleasing to God, and has split your unity with the sword of his malice.
Perhaps he is exulting over your steadfastness because of his sudden victory. I tremble, therefore [?], holy men, as I stand on Izla as though in Dothan [?],
and see chaste brothers plotting deceit against the one who was beloved by Israel, lifting him out of his cell as though out of a pit,
and sending him far away, as though to Egypt, under an unjust anathema. If only it were he alone!
But there is also the one who showed compassion like Reuben [?], and the one who devised a plan like Judah. My heart is broken over these things.
Pangs have shaken it, especially because hatred is still increasing.
This evil is pleasing to them, and without awareness the sons of Jacob persist in the passion within their breasts.
They do not look ahead to the revelation in Egypt, before the day of shame from which there is no escape.
Know, then, brothers, that the exposure of your downfall is more disgraceful to discerning people than theirs. Friends are grieved,
while enemies laugh. More than anyone else, I am tormented by the prospect of the evil to come,
against which I thought I had you as trustworthy allies in the struggle.
But now there are faltering hands and trembling, weakened thoughts. Who, then, will ask the sick for health?
Who will ask the weak for strength? And who will ask the divided for unity?
Or who would not lose hope, especially when he sees the leaders in battle being miserably trampled by one another?
If only they were adopting a position that corresponded to the cause of the disturbance! Then perhaps the evil would have been easy to deal with.
Instead, blindly and as though in darkness, they mar one another's beauty. Is not the faith of the persecuted man the very same as yours?
Perhaps even more so. Does not the one who was persecuted have the very same love—perhaps even more so?
Does not the one who was persecuted have the very same zeal—perhaps even more so?
Does not the one who was persecuted have the very same struggles for the faith—perhaps even more so?
Is there not the very same power of speech and argument in appeals on behalf of the truth, against those who once pressured you to fall away from the truth—perhaps even more so?
And how, my lords, can your struggle be [?], when you clearly have no grounds for division in the schism you have caused? But perhaps
you will say, “He was expelled by the leaders of the church, and therefore we too will reject him.” But you ought to have investigated [?].
For until now you had been suffering together with one another, and as members of one body you ought to have maintained an orderly harmony.
For if you had wished, you could have shown the metropolitan and the patriarch the strength of your love through a peaceable appeal.
And if repentance together with your brothers had been necessary, in whatever form the leaders of the church considered appropriate,
you ought to have shown yourselves ready and eager on behalf of the one who was deposed, especially since you yourselves are implicated in the very same charge.
But now, not only did you fail to hasten to [?], so as to obtain peace for yourselves from the patriarch,
but you did not even trouble the metropolitan with appeals on his behalf. Instead, you acted as befits a bitter disposition that harms without cause.
And while he was being deposed by the leaders of the church on another charge, you added other unjust accusations, pouring vinegar on the sinews.
Do you not know that your end will be bitter [?], if not now, then on the day of reckoning? Therefore wake up, holy men!
And consider that we stand on the brink of [?]. We are like water poured out on the ground that cannot be gathered up.
For among all the satanic [?], there is nothing that is not within your power to overcome, if you wish.
Nor is there any transgression that cannot be corrected, if you are willing to take care. Nor is there any stumbling block that will not yield to persuasion, if you love peace.
Therefore make peace with one another and investigate the cause of the disturbance. See whether it comes from
the working of error or from human inclination [?]. For if you think carefully, you can discern what is pleasing to God.
Do it, and live. Refrain from fury and rest from anger. Do not [?] to do evil, because evildoers will perish.
But those who hope in the Lord will inherit the earth. Know, moreover, that when the demon [?] of anger takes control of the mind,
it first strips a person of every virtue, and then it can harm his fellow even in small matters.
He cannot distinguish what is honorable from what is shameful, or benefit from harm. Instead, like a madman, he rushes headlong only to do evil.
Therefore be on your guard, brothers, lest you find yourselves bound by such an evil. For I have heard that you have already done
something that moves discerning people to cry out in distress. For, as people say, you have ratified the sentence against your brothers in an unjust document.
Alas, alas for this grievous injustice! Alas for this barbarous tyranny! Alas for this lawless wickedness!
Who, then, dared to commit this injustice? Had he previously dared to do anything else worthy of God's praise?
Did he stir his thoughts to reflect against the heresies that fight against the truth? Did he shake the standing among people of those who corrupt virtuous conduct?
Did he rebuke, in writing and in speech, those who strive under various guises to bring empty errors into God's church?
Or was this alone his first and last undertaking: to give a wicked demonstration of his zeal against his brothers and his mother's sons?
Even the mouths of their enemies are compelled to proclaim the praise of their integrity.
If, then, all of you, O merciful men, agreed to commit this injustice,
give thanks for God's gift: he did not give you authority in his church over the innocent sheep.
Otherwise, you would readily have injured those who need correction, if this is the patient kindness you show in correcting your brothers.
But if it was one man who dared to do this, and all of you were persuaded to agree,
this affair gives us reason to expect the worst: he is going to harm you greatly in other matters too, through your agreement with every evil, and, before these other things,
through the disgraceful contempt from Babai son of Yoyan, which you have either already suffered or will soon suffer, as I think.
This man has, until now, greatly disrupted the ways of the Lord, and your own ways as well.
But now, encouraged by the eagerness of your zeal, he is going to mock even more fiercely even the saints who have fallen asleep in Christ.
They left you the paths of their virtue as worthy heirs. Yet now they are going to suffer ill-treatment from you, as though they were accursed fools,
because, that is, they were unable to attain, as you have, the surpassing wisdom that you have attained. For this reason they are truly both blessed and wretched.
Blessed, indeed, because they were perfected in all the glory of virtue through their struggles for righteousness and departed to our Lord;
but wretched because they left sons like these as heirs to their monasteries.
I was compelled to say these things by the painful grief that gripped me when I heard what you had done.
Yet I do not think it possible that this evil should overcome the whole community of your brotherhood as though it were weak,
and that there should not be found among you even a few who love peace together with truth and counsel what is good. But if—God forbid—over all of you
this evil has gained mastery, like sleep over those sunk in slumber, listen to me, I beg you, if only as a voice to awaken you from your sleep.
Awake, then, awake, my brothers! Awake eagerly, as in the former days.
Clothe yourselves with the strength of the Lord's arm. Do not throw away the confidence you have, for a great reward is reserved for it.
Remember, then, the former days, when you endured a great struggle through sufferings for the truth.
Through insults and suffering, you became a public spectacle, and you also joined in solidarity with those who endured these things.
And you joyfully endured the arrogance of the powerful, because you know that you have a better and lasting reward in heaven.
Satan, the common enemy, schemes to strip you of all this glory of virtue [?].
Although he devised many schemes over the course of years, he could not harm you through the hands of outsiders as he wished.
Indeed, he constantly stirred up many people against you, people who were powerful and successful in the world.
They came to nothing, as they did, while you have remained as you were, with even greater glory, until now.
Nor was that hater of humanity able to establish among your own people a servant suited to his wishes, until he went far away from you.
He found himself a leprous demon named Isaac, stirred him up with the smoke of his wickedness, and introduced him into your peaceful community, to his own destruction and your harm.
In this man, as in a zealous servant, Satan, the enemy of our race, found ample fulfillment of his desire, and expects [?].
Therefore, may the Lord not grant the wicked one his desire through your hands, holy men, and may his scheme not succeed. Instead, may the wickedness of his lips cover him, so that with the coals
of his sin he may burn. Shake yourselves free of the dust of hatred, cleanse yourselves of the sand of hostility, and awaken from the sleep of negligence.
Therefore, live as children of [?]. Persevere in the truth of God, so that God may persevere with you, and carefully guard what your fathers entrusted to you.
Then you will be heirs to their holiness and will not be ashamed before them on the day of testing. Go out after your brothers and gather them together.
And if it is necessary to suffer for them, do not hold back until you have made them your fellow residents and partners in love.
For an evil time is about to rise against us before long, a time in which you will need many helpers,
if you are lovers of faith and lovers of truth, and if you have not lost all your virtues at once.
Therefore, my sons, remember me in my lowliness, your partner in love, and [?] kindly, just as I also treat you kindly.
Send me a written reply expressing your true thoughts about everything I have written to you. Write to me as you see fit,
whether all of you together or each one individually. For even now I am to you what I was before:
a son and a brother, poor in every respect, and a partner in your deeds and words—in everything that pleases the will of God
and delivers from wickedness everyone who calls on the name of the Lord. May he, in his grace, perfect you in every good work, so that you may do his will. Stand firm in our Lord.
18. To the brothers in his monastery, concerning the appointment of the superior.
To the lovers of God, my beloved and dear brothers: Simeon,

John, Qamisho, Bar Denha, Daniel, Bar Zasorin, Bar Nun, Ishozekha, Aphnimaran, and all the holy brothers in the monastery of Beth Abe, each by name and all equally: greetings in our Lord from Isho'yahb, your brother.
I had been expecting, brothers, that through the eagerness of your love I would receive news of that holy superior’s glorious departure from this bodily life to the harbor of eternal life.
And were it not that I fully respect the community's custom and am deeply bound by affection for my upbringing,
I might easily have taken offense at such contempt—not because of rank and title, but because of brotherhood and the upbringing to which I am accustomed.
Therefore, brothers who love God, may our Lord forgive and pardon the ways in which you have fallen short in this matter of the law of divine love.
And may he strengthen your hearts in the love of truth at all times. Amen. Now, concerning what I have heard—that the matter of leadership is still being tossed about among you by doubts,
and that you did not immediately and firmly establish what our holy father handed down to you by his spoken word as a lasting testament,
but that even now other preferences are being entertained among you—I longed to come to you myself, so that we might deliberate together about what would benefit the community
and glorify God's holy name. But since I was unable to do this, because I had already set out on my journey to the patriarch,
I thought it right to address you through an urgent letter, according to the law of spiritual love.
Remember me, then, holy men, as one who shares in your love and was brought up in your customs.
For I think it is necessary to recall these things, since the affairs of brotherhood are evidently in a sickly state. Has
the title of bishop made me a stranger to you? Has ordination to the priesthood separated me from fellowship with the community? Has a change of place produced a change of mind?
Has any one of you ever thought or spoken or [?] more than I about things that benefit the community and increase God's glory?
I speak foolishly: in whatever any one of you dares to boast concerning things appropriate to your rank and honor, I too dare to boast,
and not in equal measure, but in a way that is more praiseworthy. Why, then, in this present matter, which deserves attention more than anything else,
were you so overcome by habitual negligence that you failed to summon me, your brother, to the community's deliberations at the proper time?
For I also possessed the living testament that our holy father delivered from his blessed mouth in a firm declaration a few days before his death,
concerning the man fit to take his place in ministry—the very man about whom, as I have heard, he also gave instructions on the day of his death.
For he feared that death might suddenly overtake him and prevent him from saying what he intended to do. So he told me privately beforehand about this matter,
for he did not think that you would consent to do anything after his death without me, as you have now done, blinding yourselves to what is required.
While I was keeping our blessed father's declaration in mind so that I might relate it at the proper time, God's grace, which led him peacefully along the path of life,
gave him the peace of mind to tell it to you also on the day of his death. Thus, as far as he is concerned, you are in lasting peace.
And even now he himself is your head and guide, when you peacefully accept as your head
and guide the man whom he himself chose and appointed as your head. Therefore, let no one suppose that he departed leaving him without the hidden armor of prayer.
Rather, from the moment he set his heart on him and designated him by word, he entrusted him, the disciple of his holiness, into God's hands.
And if anyone willingly estranges himself from this man's care, there is reason to fear that he may lose the help of the righteous man's prayer.
But if he should even entertain a contrary thought, to which discerning person would this not be offensive and disturbing, besides being a passion that torments the soul,
assailing it to no good purpose? Far be this from the pure children of the righteous father and from the chaste disciples of the holy superior,
and from my beloved brothers and those brought up under my care: may they never entertain anything of this sort, nor may it be heard among them,
but only things that are good and lead to life, that benefit the community and bring praise to the Lord’s name.
Therefore, my beloved brothers, take care of your God-loving brother, the priest Mar John, whose proven virtue, over nearly seventy years, [?].
Thirty of those years were spent in blameless solitude, and the preceding years in the disciplined conduct of the school. And to you—or rather, to the elderly and honored man among you—
he was a receptive pupil in fellowship with our blessed father. And now, in addition to all these things, he has been crowned, by our father’s command, with the crown of leadership.
Receive him, then, in the Lord with all joy, as someone set apart by God through an excellent choice, as pure children of God.
With your hands and your lips, but above all with your hearts, support him in carrying out his leadership, with God’s help. And may the God of peace be with you
and establish you unshaken in the dwelling where you sojourn, all the days of your lives. And may Christ dwell in your inner being
through faith, and in your hearts through love, with your root and foundation firmly established,
so that, together with all the saints, you may attain the hope of eternal life, through the grace and mercy of our Lord Jesus Christ,
to whom be glory forever. Amen. But because the enemy of our blessings is accustomed to sow the seeds of his deceit in pure fields,
there is reason to fear that he may sow opposition to harmony among you too, as he did among the company of the apostles.
Therefore, my brothers, take care that if any of you is overtaken by such folly and disrupts your harmony by refusing obedience to the God-loving superior,
who has been set apart for you by our Lord, you who are spiritual should restore him in a spirit of gentleness, until he is freed from Satan’s snare, in which he was caught to do Satan’s will.
And may you be perfect in one spirit for works of righteousness, just as you were called in the one hope of your calling, to God’s own glory and to our encouragement.
But since I am aware of the many difficulties that commonly arise in matters like these, and also because I am not remaining here
so that I could examine, as far as I am able, each of the opposing difficulties that arise among you and apply helpful remedies,
I am therefore compelled to write you a brief statement, not as a superior or someone in authority, but as an older brother:
If anyone contends against the God-loving superior who has been appointed for you by our master’s command, according to God’s will, he must not remain in the community of Beth Abe,
lest he disturb his brothers and harm himself. Rather, he should leave quietly and peacefully, without anger, for a place where he can find rest and benefit.
And if, through lack of understanding, he should happen to speak against this statement on my account, saying, “Who
is this man who commands us to do these things?” he will afterward learn from the events themselves and be persuaded, if he fears God.
Perhaps he will also need a little repentance to attain the confidence of those who live in peace. This, after the greeting, [?].
And afterward, build one another up. Let these few things I have written to you suffice to show you my heartfelt longing for your welfare.
My whole concern is this: that you should conduct yourselves well and speak well, that God should be glorified through you, and that I too should rejoice.
Concerning this matter, I have informed our God-loving father, my lord the metropolitan, by letter of what was appropriate.
I also intend to inform our father, my lord the patriarch, in person, with God's help.
Now that you too know these things, strive together to preserve [?] the unity of the Spirit in the bond of peace.
Excel in the Lord's work [?]. May he, in his grace, make you perfect in every good work, so that you may do his will at all times. Amen.
Pray also for me, that I may spend the remainder of my days living in a way that pleases God's will.
19. A brief exhortation to someone newly appointed to lead a monastery.
To our chaste and God-loving, honored brother, Mar Qamisho: Ishoʿyahb sends greetings in our Lord. I received and read the letter you sent.
I also rejoiced at the arrival of the brothers who came to me, and I thanked our Lord for your preservation. As for fulfilling your request that I come there,
many affairs have delayed me, together with the obstacles in the way. But if a door is opened to me
in the Lord, I am ready to come. As for the things that, through the expectation of disturbance, wear down the community's spirit, as you wrote to me:
do not be quickly shaken, like people without experience or with little hope. For he is faithful to his words and generous to everyone who calls upon him—but only with wholehearted devotion.

As for what was written: if someone, in accordance with the request, [?], make separate arrangements for his reception. But if otherwise, and together with the community, make arrangements that way too.
And concerning what you also wrote to me about your own weakness in the service of the brotherhood entrusted to you: do not be at all disheartened by the difficulties that arise.
For it is not through our own [?] that our ways prosper, even if we are very diligent,
but through him who has the power to do for us far beyond everything, and beyond what we ask or imagine.
Therefore, do not be shaken by either a word or a voice, if you have undertaken to make yourself the servant of many. Instead, bear up, persevere, and be patient.
Even if you are pressed as far as Ezekiel was, the world will not be rid of such things as long as we are all human beings and children of the earth.
It is possible to benefit and to benefit others—or rather, to give life and to receive life—when the rule of the Spirit guides you and those under you.
And if anyone stumbles, the Lord heals him. For those who belong to peace and who desire to live are known.
The Lord also knows those who are his. Hope in him, then, and keep his way, and he will exalt you to inherit the earth.
Turn toward the Lord the hope you place in any human being, and you will live. As for the account of the chaste conduct of our blessed father, which you urged me to write,
I am prevented from doing this for the present. For I have no free time because of the many daily interruptions.
This work of writing requires peace of mind. As for that neighbor about whom you wrote to me,
If you do not rebuke him, take care of his affairs from now on, lest, once his root is firmly established, he trouble you every day. The one who can put this right, if he wishes,
is the metropolitan alone. If he neglects it, as is his custom, know that he desires your distress.
From now on, one of two things must be done: either endure the trial, or [?] after the patriarch. Whichever of them you choose, choose quickly.
For everything else, be on your guard, and again be on your guard. Be especially on your guard, and always be on your guard. Stay well, and pray for me.
[?]. A reply to two persons who wrote to him, one in the other's name.
To the lover of God, my lord Yazdshapur, who excels nobly through what is noble: Ishoyahb sends greetings in our Lord.
To you, then, lover of God, before I write to the person who wrote what I read, I express my praise for the zeal of your reproaches, since you feel so warmly in accordance with the law of love.
That is, you long for the birth even before the labor pains. Look, from a distance both are easy.
For the mother, however, not only when the order is reversed, but even in the proper order, it is dangerous and difficult. For it is easy to desire what is good, as it is written.
It is not easy to do it, as this too is written. But so that we do not grow weary from saying too much about such things, let us speak plainly about the matter at hand.
Was it your wish, wise man, that we should take the stone on which the spiritual building is founded at the northern [?] corner,
and hurl it, as with a sling, against a fissured cliff, and await the painful crash, which the sense of hearing conveys from a distance, as it does to the blind?
Or perhaps not this, but rather that, by rebuking the babbling [?] with the files of patience,
we should secure for our action the flight that befits it? I think wisdom is praised for this—unless complete failure is beyond reproach.
But I think you believe that, in these [?], there is no reason to accuse my conscience of envy.
And let me assure you that no opposing force is pressing upon some of us—or indeed upon all of us—to impair the goodness of our original intention.
From now on, help with every good thought that brings what you love to fulfillment.
For if you take care to do so, you can obtain convincing proof in action from all of us at the time of [?]. But for you, these words, spoken with feeling, are enough.
But to you who vigorously unravel love's accusation through dialectical reasoning,
how far will you go in silence, even to the point of reproaches? Or why did you not begin with the cause, treating the suffering as your own?
For that praiseworthy journey required you to become a close partner in the struggle, and to be a tongue for some,
a soul for others, a voice for the community, and, on your own behalf, a payer of the debt that is acknowledged.
If, through all these things, the struggle now confronting us reaches its conclusion, thanks be to God for the gift.
But if things remain as they are now, you would no longer appear free from reproach, but rather a loud-voiced accuser.
So, lest by your letter you gain relief from me from the burden of your many reproaches, while my poverty—that is, the faintheartedness of the fathers of the community—suffers loss,
Or perhaps, again, a feeble reconsideration of what was clearly explained, clearly heard [?], clearly spoken, and thoroughly examined. For this reason, with that
very same sword of rebuke, suffer freely from a free tongue, you free man. Why, then, do you regard servitude to the church of God as a disgrace? Then the action itself is also disgraceful.
But God forbid! Turn instead to the spiritual book, and you will find its praise. What, then, comes next?
As for the one who lies in ambush beside the road and bites the heel to bring down the honored, what, in your view, is the wound that has befallen our God-loving brother John?
So that those who know him should no longer regard him as beloved and praiseworthy, but as disgraced and despised.
Oh, what cruelty! For in a single stroke you have thrown him into Satan’s fetters and portrayed us as servants of sin.
And because of the opponent who pressed against him, you have proclaimed the work of God an evil ministry. Let its own rebuke suffice for this, as it is said:
“Let the [?] be in its [?].” What, then, comes next? “I want,” he says, “to know the reason for this person’s rejection.”
Are you seeking a mother for a child who does not exist? Or do you call a delay in administration rejection? But I would not regard it that way even
if someone else were brought forward in this man’s place for the ministry that had been prepared. Even then I would not consider this man rejected.
For I see Joseph, called Barsabbas, who was surnamed Justus, among the apostles, even though he was not numbered among the Twelve.
And if not in that case, how much less when even that has not happened! And what comes next?
“The agreement of certain people alone,” he says, “who are blameless in their profession of Christianity would have sufficed.”
I too say that it would have sufficed, if you had been trusted in what you ought to have been trusted with, even if not in other things.
But when two or three of those who agree are nearby, even if they are people of lesser reputation, so that it would not be for the empty air that the representative was anointed,
but, through the few who are nearby, for the multitude of others who are far away. Otherwise, who would advise completing it without being found to have erred?
And what comes next? “I do wish to know, even secretly, the faults that were found.” I tell you openly that it is not difficult to find such a thing in our nature.
But the Lord of our nature does not reject the sinful human race from the ministry of his church. And what comes next?
“If,” he says, “one or several of those entrusted with [?] held up its completion, they ought [?] to have turned away from what was supposed.”
Half the doubt is indeed reasonable, but not all of it. For here, out of compassion, I am healing the sore of presumption.
And you will concede to me that there was no adversary, no evil occurrence, and no counsel foreign to the fear of God. And what comes next?
“I am looking,” he says, “at the hidden things that are to come [?]. Show me the outcome of the affairs that you previously said were going to happen.”
The whole abundance of objections against me has vanished at once, and the blame that brings hatred has remained with the one who admits that the promises have not been fulfilled.
But I, as a human being, planted in hope, and as a human being I water in hope.

But it is God who makes such a planting fruitful, who gives fruit to the farmer’s hope. And if, he says, when he brings it to completion, we [?] it in keeping with the purpose, thanks for accepting it.
But if it is contrary to the aim and otherwise, prepare even so to manage it. And again, what then?
“Persevere,” he says, “in completing the foundation you have laid, so that there may be no opportunity for [?] tongues to pour out their customary reproaches.”
And by acting in what way, then, do you suppose we shall escape reproaches like these as free men? For just as the tongue is ready for this, so
the accusing tongue is ready for that as well—and both, that is, in return for kindness. Or which of the godly have you ever seen escape tongues like these?
The fathers? The apostles? The prophets? Our Lord? His Father? Clearly, not even one. There is enough consolation, then, for sinners in things like these.
But these words are for you, you contemptible accuser, in response to those words with which, as with a rod of love, you were chastising the one you love in your letter.
As for what happened, how it happened, and why it happened: if you have heard what was openly said [?], be assured that the hidden things are the same.
Or if you wish to know more, my mouth will speak with yours, God willing. But for now let us concern ourselves only with this:
that, as far as possible, despite our weakness, we may secure the undertaking from there, our God-loving brother, Mar John. For even if the fulfillment is not complete,
but partial [?]—at least a portion of these things—be assured and believe that no foreign thought is troubling the conscience of those appointed to this.
As I also wrote once before, make every effort yourself as well, [?], since we wish to please the will of God.
And may the merciful God himself, who always does for us more than we ask or imagine,
bring the labor of our diligence to completion in a manner worthy of the glory of his name. Stand firm in our Lord.
21. To the same person, on the same subject, from the same person. Many greetings.

We judged well, even if we were judged well. But that we left nothing for the Spirit is not very good—indeed, not good at all. It is right, that is, for us to be reproached when we hold back any of our strength;
but when we expend it all in the contest set before us, we are already victorious in the arena [?], even if we do not yet possess the crown itself.
The contest, then, my friends, is spiritual, and its fruit is spiritual too. And often it can be found reproving zeal.
Whose zeal? That of those who have been entrusted by the Spirit himself with the vision of hidden things. And who knows whether, as with Samuel, he is also reproving us—
he who [?]—in these matters? And this is if the opponent who stands against us succeeds, though perhaps he cannot succeed, as I still hope.
For how could someone who has God oppose the fear of God, contrary to his conscience, in matters that inspire fear?
Unless perhaps he is overcome by shame—that shame of which it is also said that it produces sins—
and through it, as through the compulsion of faintheartedness, is swept into disgraceful subjection.
When I thought that it was because of this that he had been brought to the decision he reached, I wrote him something appropriate in response to my summons to ordination.

And it was not only appropriate, but also useful for him to find a spiritual way out without completing it, if he wishes to make use of it. But if he turns aside from the path of the fear of God into the distraction of cowardice,
he does well to disregard what I have written and to act alone in doing things that he does not [?] to do.
It is good for us, too, to witness wicked deeds only from a distance, through hearsay alone. Put your hope in the Lord, then, holy men.
And if some hostile action should come from certain people, keep yourselves from the stumbling that inevitably occurs in such circumstances, remembering that we are dust.
It swells with pride now and is scattered shortly afterward. Pray that we may always be found worthy of mercy, and may God's grace guide us in everything. The end.
22. To the honored and distinguished friend of God, Mar Yazdegerd. Isho'yahb: peace in our Lord.
Amid the rush [?] of worthy activities, your letter reached me, lover of God. And as the beauty of its reading carried me far away,
I remained as though asleep, until, with God's help, I established the divine sanctuary in the midst of a field of weeds.
After being overcome by much drowsiness, I returned to my lodging. Immediately, before attending to necessary business, I read your letter again.
I praised its contemplation of the soul and its movements, and of the body and its habits, up to the point of its illustration.
But when it was swept away toward a subject of praise, I felt as though struck, because it was being forcibly diverted, as though away from the truth, toward an alien likeness.
Why, lover of wisdom, did you carelessly bestow on me, as though on someone else, the gift of empty praise?
For someone in whom wisdom rests—if that is how you regarded me—the simple sincerity of a noble gift from a lover of wisdom would have been enough.
In this way, genuine and firm trust would be placed in that exalted goodness, shown by it with generosity of soul toward a weak man.
Apart from this, however, I gladly accepted the reverence of your humility, lover of wisdom. I acknowledge that you have rightly taken precedence in a matter of virtue.
The birthright is therefore yours in that in which the spiritual law has placed the perfection of virtue.
For my part, apart from precedence in position, I fall short in everything. Yet I was troubled when I turned back to my own understanding, by the things in which, harshly but in a consoling manner,
I was wronged, even though the charms of false praise are pleasant to my weak soul.
But love of goodness persuaded you, lover of wisdom, to let yourself be misled a little by a false report,
and much of the abundance of love was poured out in such gifts toward a weak man, one greatly despised by his own conscience.
But since I am quite bewildered by the ways in which others see me differently, I confess to God concerning myself that I am wretched and enslaved to the passions.
But to your God-loving soul, which longs so deeply for goodness, may our Lord in his mercy grant a sure hope.
For if this happens, I will not be put to shame, goodness will not be troubled, expectation will not be overturned, and love will not change.
Nor will the choice prove false, nor will joy be taken away. Instead, everything in every way will be praise of God, who—as you have beautifully shown—joined the soul
to this body, such as it is, and united them in a marvelous bond. He made the hidden beauty of rationality perceptible.
He enabled goodness in its many forms to be known through a single goodness. He transformed this perceptible vessel by a power reaching into what is hidden.
He enabled us to know and marvel at ourselves in everything, and everything in us, and, in us, the unity of his creative power.
He who never left himself without a witness among us, so that his goodness might not be stolen away from us through error and deceptive silence;
he who formerly appeared in visions, afterward spoke with a voice, and at times spoke a word in the depths of the mind’s stillness;
and finally, in a real and complete body, chose to preserve the goodness within us unimpaired;
he who gathered the many different forms of virtue under one lofty and glorious head and named it love; he who through this has now raised you
above my lowliness and granted you the first approach by letter; he who gave me the second place to keep in the exchange of inquiries about your welfare—
may the hidden power of his compassion bring the beginning of our fellowship to completion through growth in his spiritual law, to the praise of his holy name.
May he, through his [?], perfect our weakness in every good work, so that we may do his will all the days of our lives. Amen. Give my humble greetings to whomever you wish,
especially to those who are pleasing to our Lord, and particularly to those whose greetings you conveyed to me individually in your letter.
And may the peace of God, which surpasses all understanding, keep your hearts blameless until the day of our Lord Jesus Christ. End.
23. To the truly faithful and God-fearing Mar Isho'sabran: Isho'yahb sends greetings in our Lord.
I received with joy the letter of your love, O lover of God, and thanked our Lord for your good health, and greatly for the richness of your faith.
You also made me rejoice greatly. For this wealth has distinguished the generous in every generation. But that upon a weak and feeble man such as I am
your wise judgment should rest in this way did not greatly move me to rejoice—that is, not at all.
For someone whose open confidence is beaten down by the burden of his sins, it is praise enough that he is not spoken of as badly as his wickedness deserves—if he can endure even this without danger.
And is it not dangerous for us to be known to God in one way but regarded by people in another? Nevertheless, I was persuaded to lessen a little my anxious uncertainty,
because I attributed to the skilled scribe who served you through his craft in writing the letter to my humble self the lofty opinion
that was bestowed upon me as though upon someone [?], through a mistaken impression of excellence.
But may our Lord in his mercy grant that your faith may be established upon the foundation of truth, and that a hope of fulfillment may be given to the eager desires expressed in your letter.
For if God’s grace attends to these things, he will graciously make me also worthy of deliverance from the misery of condemnation.
And may he graciously grant us, from the great wealth of God’s compassion, to find joy together at the proper time in the fulfillment of virtues.
May he in his mercy strengthen our weakness to do his will all the days of our lives. End.
24. To our father, holy in every way, the venerable Mar Isho'yahb, Catholicos and Patriarch: your son Isho'yahb sends greetings in our Lord.
Let the fear of God within you understand, O our venerable father, that the good seed which for a long time was being choked by brushwood and thorns,

now that it has been cleared and has sprouted through your fatherly care at this time, has begun to rejoice in the light of heavenly things and is preparing for God’s angels the joy spoken of in the Gospel.
For Shapur, who until now was being bent down by the bonds of error into the depths of faintheartedness,
And he could not look properly toward the heights of heavenly things with the boldness of confession [?]. But now the help of God, through the right hand of your fatherhood,
has released him from such bonds and shown him to be free from slavery to destruction. And now, walking freely,
in this great house, which until now had seemed cramped to him, and with a new soul, that is, and a body prepared to suffer,
he made the good confession before many witnesses and stirred the assembly of those who fear God to praise the Most High.
Therefore Christ’s holy Church here, which is served by the sinful man that I am, also stretched out her hands and received him.

And through participation in the life-giving mysteries she gave him the hidden power that sanctifies all, so that through it the sickness of despair and the pain of destructive anxiety might be driven away from the person in question,
and he might become a herald of God’s glory and of a triumphant confession. Immediately afterward, he hurried to go to the theater that is now nearby,
so that there he might receive whatever the merciful God, in his compassion, wished to provide for him.
Let your fatherhood therefore rejoice in what has happened, and pray earnestly that the outcome of everything may be crowned with glory to God.
And may the merciful God himself, who holds in his hands every good gift with which to enrich those who fear him,
