bring your fatherhood’s labor to completion in every good work, to the praise of his holy name at all times. Amen. End.
25. To our father, holy in all things, the reverend Mar Catholicos, the patriarch. Give your blessing. Ishoʿyahb: greetings in our Lord.
The cup of our afflictions has apparently reached its brim, our God-loving father, and our means of deliverance have been blocked at the exits from distress.
Even a place of refuge has vanished, as it is written, and there is no one to call the tormentors to account.
For the great swarm of worms that the evil overseer bred from the common body over a long time and wickedly strengthened
has already overcome most of its parts, as can be seen, and has now crawled all together toward the head of the whole body,
where our mind also—that is, the mind of God’s Church—is established by God’s command, so that it may finish off the remainder of the multitude with its customary destruction.
And perhaps, after it has consumed everyone, it will consume him too, and the world will rest from its misery. If, then, you are still alive amid these things, as we hope, our father,
and if you are well, as we also pray, and if, by God’s grace, some consolation in spirit and body remains for your fatherhood,
then, if anyone is coming, please have a letter written to me, so that perhaps I too may find relief from the burdens of sorrow, even through a breath of refreshment.
For matters here are being put somewhat in order with God’s help, as the times allow. Yet I am still being provided for in a way that runs counter to the times,
and the providence of God’s grace guides my weakness above the miseries of the times.
It would be a wonder if I escaped here from the end that my sins deserve. For concerning what awaits me there, I have no doubt.

I therefore beg your fatherhood to pray that I may be deemed worthy of mercy and find the grace of repentance sufficient to heal my wounds, before I reach that state of helplessness which leaves many bewildered.
And may the God of peace grant your fatherhood a peaceful life at all times, together with everything pleasing to his will, all the days of your life.
26. Isho‘yahb, deacon of the [?] of God in [?].
To the God-loving brothers, the monks on Mount Alfaf, who in a humble spirit offer the sacrifice of virtuous conduct
to God who is above all, through our Lord Jesus Christ: may peace increase among you. I, my God-loving brothers,
confident that the power of our Lord’s commandment works effectively in you too, as in the rest of those who fear God, have chosen to write to you with a peaceful conscience,
eager to receive an account of your conduct, not from the mouths of strangers but from a hand belonging to your own community,
so that my confidence in you may remain secure in the times to come. For it is not possible, in my opinion, nor beneficial,
for someone who truly worships Christ not to be filled with the love of Christ. For this is the sign of discipleship among Christians.
Nor is it possible for someone who establishes in himself this spiritual law—the great love that our Lord taught—not to be humble and wise.
Nor is it possible or conceivable that someone who, with such great humility, has made this great commandment the foundation of his actions should not be peaceful and gentle.
How indeed can someone attain virtue in any other way, when through fleshly deeds he has acquired what is opposed to virtue?
For anger [?], violence, hostility, abusive speech, harboring evil in the mind, wickedly coveting another person’s inheritance,
attacking the boundary established by the fathers with tongue and hand, claiming to be righteous—as madmen imagine—by insulting the brotherhood, and other things like these:
I do not think these constitute a praiseworthy portion for the worshippers [?] of God, nor perhaps even for those who possess a natural conscience within a pagan soul.
Therefore, let anyone who does not show everyone through the fruits of the Spirit that he is Christ’s disciple stop thinking that he is one. But for someone to proclaim [?] about
himself that he is virtuous, and not merely to praise himself but also to interpret other people’s actions maliciously—such a person is, I think, sufficiently rebuked by his own conscience,
unless it has been corrupted by the sickness of seeking precedence. Discerning people also regard him as ignorant and without understanding,
because he thinks that he acquires not grounds for boasting from his deeds, but deeds from his boasting. It is good, therefore, my God-loving brothers,
to leave the praise of our deeds to the mouths of others, if those deeds cannot be hidden altogether, as our Lord commanded.
For our part, let this alone be worthy of our concern: to believe the truth and practice the truth,
and to teach the truth, without showing ourselves in any way to be among those who boast about themselves.
Instead, through the open display of the truth, let us make ourselves known to all human minds before God.
In this way, let us give no cause for stumbling to Jews, pagans, or the church of God. Let us consider how to walk carefully, not as fools,
but as wise people who make the most of their time. The rule of virtue commands me, my brothers, to listen together with you to these apostolic appeals—
that rule whose author is none other than the holy apostle—
so that, as far as it rests with me, every cause of stumbling may be removed.
But how can it be removed, except by my enduring the insolence of fools with great kindness and patience?
The fact is that someone belonging to your company has now chosen to act insolently, with a foolish mind.
For this man, driven from the labor of monastic life as though by an enemy, was compelled to hide in a desolate cave.
And when, from [?], this man, driven from the labor of monastic life as though by an enemy, was compelled to hide in a desolate cave.
And when he fled from the discipline shared with his brothers and from obedience to his superiors, he hid in a solitary rocky retreat.
And when he departed from a blameless way of life, he preferred to dwell in a cave that causes stumbling

and live there. It is enough that a rich place should be found ready in every way for someone who rejoices in turmoil among people. As for this man, then, who has chosen to stir up this untimely and unprofitable conflict,
and is eager to trade in the merchandise of stumbling through harmful disturbance, brothers who love God, I have sent him a brotherly appeal three times through trustworthy intermediaries,

advising him to value the good of his soul above everything by departing from the dwelling he has seized. For if our Lord taught us to give up what belongs to us, he certainly never taught us to seize anything.
And when I had pleaded with him at length but accomplished nothing, it seemed right to me to inform you also, as wise people capable of helping him,
so that, if this affair took place without your knowledge, you would take care to put it right once you learned of it.
But if it took place with your knowledge, I too will know that he is not the only person among you who loves strife and goes astray,
but that there are others as well [?]—if, in that whole assembly of so many people, not even a few lovers of peace and counselors of good can be found.
Read, then, in your book of records, and see who is shown to have been the first inhabitant of that place that is no place.
For you can remember it well, since the affair is not yet ancient: he belonged to our fold and ended his life among us.
And his end is known to all of you. How, then, did you think it right to encroach on our boundaries?
Have the affairs of the holy church now become less important in your eyes? I do not think so.
Why, then, does that foolish man provoke contentious strife while you remain silent? Do you not know that great disturbances arise from small causes,
or do you not acknowledge that insignificant and uneducated people have thrown many wise people into confusion? Know this also:
if I had not bound the hands of the impetuous men among us with the bonds of restraint, they would have rushed with human fury against the man who acted insolently without any right.
Help, then, in the work of peace, you honorable men, and restrain the instigator of conflict from entering our boundaries.
As lovers of peace, send him away peacefully to the inheritance of your fathers. Do not give anyone any cause for stumbling.
For already I have made known to you the law of spiritual love.
And from now on I take the lead in zeal for [?] peace. By your command, put an end to this disturbance that you have stirred up.
Repay God's mercy, for you have become zealous partners in the labor of those who are zealous for him.
And then let this helpful appeal be withdrawn from you. Even so, my labor in these matters is not without fruit.
In any event, the purpose of my efforts is being fulfilled in another way, as you know. But whoever has troubled you will bear the judgment, whoever he may be.
But concerning these things I have written to you, reply to me in a letter with the truth of your thoughts about them.
For I want to learn your intention concerning God, not from someone else’s words, but from your own explanation.
Indeed, this is precisely why I wrote to you—not because I am incapable of doing what is easy even for the least of my people to do.
Rather, through concern for what is right, I am testing the sincerity of your love, and seeking to learn by experience whether you fear God in everything.
May he, in his grace, equip you with every good work to do his will. Be steadfast in our Lord. The end.
27. To our God-loving, honored brother, Mar Moses the priest: Ishoyahb, greetings in our Lord.
I received and read what you wrote, brother, and I thanked our Lord for your diligence in such matters.
But I was deeply distressed by the manner of the appeal and also by its very cause. My thoughts wandered as far as astonishment at the ink.
I was greatly amazed at the incongruity of [?]: how what then reached only the point of astonishment
has now come close even to the deed itself. For one must surely be amazed if a cedar happens to need the shade of a thornbush.
And if this present matter too is merely a form of words, why, then, was it not expressed cautiously, especially to me? But if you adopted it as a pretext,
why was the pretext not that which has been established as a sign for us all, and a source of pride for those who possess it, and in which we have also been commanded to outdo one another?
But if it is neither the one nor the other, and what was written is really and truly so—alas for the misery of this ruin!
That she who nourishes thousands at every onslaught should turn to the mother of hunger to ask for the necessities of life in a time of need!
But it has not been established, nor will it be believed, that effective help should flow in the opposite direction:
from those who hunger every day to those who are satisfied at every hour. But if, while Nisibis’s good guardian still stands ready even now
to sustain the multitude of the needy in every necessity, you, brother, with an excessive expectation—that is, of exceptional ability or exceptional concern—
send needy souls to me as to someone who possesses these qualities, know first, modest man, that you have been deceived by a false report,
if you have heard anything at all resembling what you wrote. You will be convinced that it is false if you learn, first, from the place and its customary way of life,
and then from the poverty of a dwelling deprived of everything, and again from the groaning of the afflicted—
these alone whom an evil time, in the misery of its nature, has cast upon us in the courts of the church.
They would have been enough for me to scatter among them with my own hands even Solomon’s wealth, had it been entrusted to me, if I possessed a compassionate soul. But now, instead of anything else,
an aching heart that approaches us finds only a sigh from us. And for this gift, then, the needy of Nisibis have no need, as I believe.
For that city, rich in good things, cannot be lacking in this either.
It deserves to surpass everyone in everything, and, drawing from that fountainhead which waters it, to pour out in turn a stream of assistance, in every fine form, both to us and to everyone.
Even its poverty is sufficient to enrich many, as it is written. But you have done well, our brother, in laboring to bring relief to the distressed.
You also do well if you believe that we lack wealth, and even the means for a small gift.
You do still better if you do not take offense when you hear that we are sending away empty-handed those whom you sent to us.
Let our willingness alone, eager for good, suffice you, if possible. For perhaps a [?] heart cannot be without this.
And if we attend to what is appropriate for us, it is possible for this to be accomplished in deed as well, with God's help.
May he, in his compassion, strengthen our weakness to do his will at all times, all the days of our lives. Amen. Finished.
28. To the truly faithful and God-fearing Mar Julian. Ishoyahb: greetings in our Lord.
I received your loving letter with uncertainty, lover of God.
In name it was addressed to me, but in its intention it was addressed to someone else—someone I am not.
Fear of presumption prevented me from answering on account of the name, while fear of causing offense prevented me from remaining silent on account of the intention.
When I turned from my many uncertainties to the awareness of my own poverty, I gave thanks for God's mercy, and with a weak soul joyfully received the love expressed in your esteem.
Not as I know myself, but as you have ventured to believe. For, without presumption or self-deception, I have misery in every respect and a conscience that rebukes me.
But you have a faithful soul, healthy in its love of goodness, so that even in a weak person, greatly despised by his own conscience,
you confidently place your trust in the hope of virtue. Yet although it is not fitting that the gracious faith you possess should prove fruitless,
the shaky support that I am cannot provide help. But it is within God's power even to raise the dead.
He is rich in mercy. Therefore both of us must turn in prayer to him who is mighty, with one shared sense of need.
For my part, that he may adorn your sincere faith with abundant fruits of mercy,
keep your foot from the stumbling blocks of sins and from every distressing pain, and fill you at all times with the abundance of his help.
And for your part, that the guilty person whom you have regarded in this way may turn from the sickness of guilt to the mercies of repentance,
and through this be made worthy of salvation by grace, and acquire the confidence that is hoped for.
For if this happens, thanks be to the mercy of our Lord, who, even when we neither ask nor consider it, attends to our pains in his [?].
Therefore hope in the Lord, lover of God, and [?] his way. He will raise you up to inherit the land. Turn everyone's hope toward him, and you will
live. Do not seek a model of virtues among the weak, if those whom you have regarded in this way are indeed such. Nor take offense when you do not find one.
Nor should you be misled by a false report into supposing yourself superior to those far away, as has now happened to you.
For we are all human beings and children of the earth, scattered dust and a mixture of passions, and together we fall short of the glory of God.
Indeed, it is good to be zealous for good things. Indeed, it is good to speak about good things. But it is better still to do good things.

Indeed, blessed is the one whose wrongdoing has been forgiven and whose sins have been covered. Indeed, blessed is the person whose sin the Lord will not count against him, and in whose heart there is no deceit.
Let us therefore desire with all our being to be granted this blessedness by grace, through the grace of our God, who is good and merciful forever. Amen.
The poor church of Nineveh sends greetings to your beloved self, having received your greeting in a letter.
Especially those who belong more closely to our Lord send greetings, those to whom the gift of peace has been granted in greater measure.
Convey the greetings of his humble self to all those among you who fear God, and pray for me. End.
29. Isho'yahb to John, my brother in our Lord. Peace.
Everyone calls the stirring of the mind that yearns to meet its loved ones ‘longing.’ For all these many years we have exhausted this longing over you in vain.
Now it has grown weak, and we will no longer continue to suffer the same thing through an unfulfilled hope.
Nor should you continue to give us empty promises of a visit that has not been made possible. Instead, give time its due, remain in peace, and pray for me from
afar, as indeed it is right for you to do. Write and inform me about matters that require attention, and stay well. End.
30. Isho'yahb to Narsai and Maremmeh, my brothers in our Lord. Peace.

That you should come to remember your brother [?] only under the compulsion of persuasion, my brothers, and should offer a greeting only under compulsion to a weak man who stands in such a relationship to you—
and even this barely, and after a very long delay—has happened for no other reason
than the death of undying love, through which we used to think ourselves above everyone else. For even if it has not died,
as perhaps you too will say that it has not died, it is nevertheless sick and suffering terribly: in one limb from the affliction of stumbling,
and in another from the pain of contempt. Yet thanks be to the mercy of our Lord, who from time to time renews in us the fragrance of [?] of closeness to him, as a sign of resurrection,
just as he has now stirred the virtue within you to remember in a letter someone who had long been forgotten, even though its wording was expressed in an unfamiliar manner.
But this too comes from the sickness already mentioned. For [?] also accompanies sickness, and both belong to a soul subject to suffering.
Nevertheless, even so, and for this alone, I give thanks to the grace of our Lord, who has at least preserved for us a remnant of acknowledgment in remembrances at long intervals.
I also pray that the wealth about which many were mistaken long ago may not again decline and diminish any further than this.
But how are you, really? And again, how are you [?]? I wanted to know. May our Lord in his mercy grant
that you may be as you ought to be. You too, pray for me, that I may be deemed worthy of mercy and find the grace of repentance.
which is suitable for healing my pains. And may I see you in peace, as the Lord wills. It is finished.
31. To the chaste, God-loving, holy priest, Mar Sabrisho, bishop. Ishoyahb: greetings in our Lord.
Partly the pressure of your trial, and partly the [?] sight of the common head, O lover of God, when they coincided last year,
made a meeting with you available to my weakness through God's grace. And from the testing of words [?] time.
I have good memories of you every day. I also look forward to receiving news of your affairs with a good conscience.
At last, when the son of your love, and my brother, Mar Sergius, priest and teacher, reached me, he eased my longing a little with news of your health.
And I longed to see you through him, insofar as that is possible through an exchange of greetings.
I ask you to remember me in prayer before God, each time you offer the sacrifice before him on behalf of everyone,
so that perhaps I may be able to spend the rest of my days in a life pleasing to God's will.
And whenever you find someone coming toward Assyria, write and let me know about your health, so that I may rejoice. Stay well. It is finished.
32. To God's chosen one, Mar Samuel, priest. Ishoyahb [?]: greetings in our Lord.
“Blessed is the man who takes up Christ's yoke from his youth,” says God's prophet, “and sits alone and is silent [?],
because he has taken his yoke upon himself.” For the work of righteousness is also peace, as he said, and the service
of righteousness is quietness and hope forever and ever. Therefore, whoever is like this is blessed in what he does.
Rejoice, then, in your hope, O chaste one, and persevere [?] in the good struggle for virtue that you have chosen, so that you may attain the eternal life to which you were called.
And pray for my weakness, I ask you, that I may be found worthy of the grace of repentance and find mercy before our Lord on the day of his appearing.
And I will see you [?] in person wherever God wills. Until then, remember me every day, and do not neglect this. It is finished.
33. To my dear and honored Mar John, priest.
Ishoyahb: greetings in our Lord. Speech is a distinctive beauty for bodily beings, wisdom a distinctive beauty for rational beings, and love a distinctive beauty for the wise.
All three come from the gracious gift of God: the first through nature, the second through learning,
and the third through the spiritual law. Therefore, let whoever is fully perfected in this be placed among the good things that bring perfection.
It is also good for someone to hold fast to this through an excellent choice. Since I have held fast to what I have held fast to, in the way I have held fast to it,
the fulfillment of that choice has always accompanied the choice, as it does now. For through our brother Sergius the teacher I received your loving greeting, with its sweet fragrance.
You gladdened me with news of your health, as was fitting, though not in writing, as would have been fitting. And in my joy I gave thanks to our Lord.
May it therefore please you always to do for me what befits your kindness toward me. And do not refrain from praying for me.
so that perhaps I may be able to spend the rest of my days in a life pleasing to God’s will. Stay well, and grow in love, which is your excellent possession. End. [?]
34. To our father, holy in every way, his reverence Mar the Catholicos-Patriarch. Your son Ishoʿyahb sends greetings in our Lord.

Your excellence in everything, father, deserves to increase. Even now, moved by it as is your custom, you have shown yourself toward my humble self with an abundance of remembrances, in the ardor of fatherly love.
And through five letters, as I have learned, you have offered me, weak as I am, cause for joy within a short time.
Although these did not reach me, since the adversities that arose held them back, I was nevertheless granted ample joy when I learned of the exceptional care your fatherhood has for me.
I learned more fully about the state of affairs among you, as far as was possible, from our brother Mar Ishoʿyahb the teacher.
I thank our Lord for everything, and I pray that you may be strengthened still further in our Lord, for his praise and for the honor of the whole community.
For we have been shaken a little, but we have not been abandoned completely. We too can say, by way of comparison, ‘We are troubled, but we are not forsaken.’
For the grace of the merciful God still guides my weakness beyond what my sins deserve. But because of my defiled conscience, I am troubled by daily fear.
Therefore I beg your fatherhood to pray that I may be delivered from danger to body and soul and preserved in the purity that is fitting.
And may I spend the rest of my days in a life pleasing to God’s will. End.
35. Ishoʿyahb to my beloved Hormizd.
Greetings in our Lord. If I had been the first, brother, to visit you by letter, or again, if immediately after you wrote
I had answered you, or again, if after two or three letters I had drawn back from what appeared to be negligence and had refrained from being reproached, your praise would, that is, have been less.
My joy would also have been less. But now that things have happened as they have, and you have acted as you have, greater praise is yours,
and complete joy is mine, both in their proper measure. Therefore, brother, keep overcoming me in such things at all times, and I will rejoice.
And do not grow weary of filling both me and all who love you with gifts like these, even if on our side the repayment of this praiseworthy debt falls short.
May the God of peace be with you and guide you without stumbling in everything. Pray for me also, that I may spend the rest of my days in a life pleasing to God’s will. End.
36. To the chaste and God-loving man, our honored brother Mar Alahazekha, priest and teacher. Ishoʿyahb sends greetings in our Lord.
In your case, then, lover of God, the onslaught of daily adversities
found you each day unresponsive to its bandit-like attempt to turn you away from the glorious commitments of your love and distract you into the negligence of forgetting me.
Therefore, in the very depth of [?], in the very storm of turmoil, amid the very waves of afflictions, you portrayed the duties of spiritual love with freedom of thought.
Twice you have granted the weak man that I am a praiseworthy visit by inquiring after my welfare.
And with exceptional diligence you secured for yourself the precious benefit of being the first to make an approach.
But for weak me, the mere blast of the world’s trials is enough, time and again, to distract me from
Reminders of afflictions, and of being prevented at times from the good conduct that the spiritual law requires for the duties of love—but not so in the things that happened.
For the force of such opposition was not sufficient, as [?] thought, to cause slackness without external pressure:
in the eager and earnest approach of your God-loving soul, in matters where the spiritual law demands the exercise of perfection.
But that other thing—the weariness caused by injuries—you drove away from me with God’s help.
And as for that compulsion to return far away from my place of residence, as though bound by the shackles of affliction, I was persuaded with a few words.
But through the lack of bearers of reassurance, which in any case came about, I was overcome, as I have continued to be overcome until now.
Now, however, having read the second letter, I also honor the love shown in the first through the gratitude I owe.
And I call your God-loving soul blessed, considering the purpose of your letter solely in relation to love.
But I did not like the elaborate praise in it, through which many are drawn into the snares of flattery by the habit of giving pleasure.
And on both sides they contend with the distress of conscience, unless conscience itself has also been corrupted by the disease of insensibility.
It is good, I think, for a free person moved by love to show warmth toward his friend with the openness of intimacy and complete confidence.
And the example of our [?] is enough for our understanding. Moved purely by the spirit of love,
they left spiritual models of gracious fellowship to the heirs of their labors. May we all emulate them,
and may God’s help bring us to imitate their virtue, through his grace and mercy forever. Amen. Now, concerning what you wrote to me,
brother, as you groan under the weight of the arrogance of those in high places, do not be surprised at this matter.
For, as it is written, one higher than the high watches over them. But you, hope in the Lord and keep his way, and do the work of one who renounces.
For this is your calling. A humble rebuke consumes the dust that exalts itself, and the rod of humility subdues the arrogance of the boastful.
And if not by these means, then by his own weapons. For it is possible to overcome passion with passion, as the saying goes.
And if neither this way nor that way succeeds, endure humbly, so that you may be worthy of the blessings that are written. And may God preserve you from every evil. [?]
37. To our father, holy in every respect, the reverend lord Catholicos-Patriarch. Your son Ishoʿyahb, [?], greetings.
Father [?], the zeal of your fatherly love, with its astonishing care, has far exceeded the needs of my weakness.
Neither the severity of the present affliction nor all the things capable of hindering the course of virtuous accomplishments could restrain your fatherly zeal
from continually hovering over the vessels of grace that we have all been appointed to be—and over me more than the others,
who am entirely weak, as everyone knows very well. For now, too, I have received the warmth of your fatherly love in a letter of greeting.
And I longed to hear it in peace of spirit. I thank your fatherly compassion with a humble conscience.
For I pray and strive at all times to give my longing feet rest soon by meeting you, my father, with God's help. But before

I am deemed worthy of this, visit me in your kindness, as you have until now. Always grant my weakness the gift of your prayers, so that I may spend the remainder of my days living in a way that pleases God's will. End.
38. To the chaste and God-loving bishop, our honored brother Mar Aba. Isho'yahb: greetings in our Lord.
I received your loving letter with astonishment, O lover of God. I thanked our Lord for his care for you, and under the weight of suffering I was sorrowfully [?] into the depths of discouragement.
As I recalled every danger that your holiness had undergone at the hands of the wicked, I took greater courage from the hope inspired by your endurance, and turned to praising God.
For in the severity of your afflictions I discovered the aim of your persecutors: in you, as in the embodiment of faith, they were inflicting suffering on the Lord of glory.
But I also saw the contest of your endurance: in a weak body you faced the force of the torments with the courage of heroic souls.

Your body did not, as its nature might lead it to do, succumb to the violence of the sufferings by escaping through death; nor was your soul, as its nature might lead it to be, bewildered by the prolonged terrors of every day,
and driven away from sharing the sufferings it desired by withdrawing into another kind of derangement.
Instead, with the steadfastness of your whole being, you endured the entire onslaught of the wicked with humility and patience, until the respite that seems to be lasting.
Until the limit of that abandonment which brings help; until the limit of your endurance and of the reckless onslaught of the wicked;
until the point at which God desired, in his [?], to perfect the power of his might in the frailty of your weakness. Because of these things,
therefore, my brother, you have driven the many doubts born of discouragement from my mind, and turned the sadness of my thoughts into thanksgiving to God.
And with joy I call your God-loving soul blessed, because you have been deemed worthy to share in sufferings for his truth at the beginning of a contest which, I believe, awaits many.
For the mystery of lawlessness and the revelation of the lawless one have already begun to be active, as can be seen.
[?] Many will be chosen, tested, and made white, as it is written. But blessed are you if you have fought, been tested, and come through shining.
And blessed are you even if you are still [?] in the contest itself. Still more blessed are you if you are deemed worthy of even greater things than these.
For whoever has been entrusted with little is also entrusted with much, as it is written. Rejoice, then, in your hope, O blessed one.
And be renewed in the spirit of your faith, as is fitting for you. For already you also have the confidence that comes from suffering
to ask in prayer for mercy and help for the church of God. Pray, then, also for this [?] church of ours,
and for all those who take refuge in it, who together have wished to share gladly with you in voluntary sufferings.
Through me they all appeal to you—the baptized believers together with the unbaptized believers—to repay them, in spiritual love, with prayer in return for the blessing of the linen cloth.
Pray also for my weakness, I ask you, so that I may be deemed worthy of the grace of repentance and find mercy before our Lord,
and spend the remainder of my days living in a way that pleases God's will. End.
39. To our father, holy in every way, the venerable Mar Catholicos and Patriarch. Give your blessing. Isho'yahb: greetings in our Lord.
Until now, our father, the hope of your coming here, together with my own eagerness to come there, had eased the pain of separation in my innermost mind.
But now that the difficulties of the times have frustrated both these things, sorrow spreads within me, adding grief each day.
For this reason, then, we must now once again use the customary means of written letters to console the sorrow within us,
until the Lord turns toward us and has mercy on us, and the light of his salvation shines forth in grace. Nevertheless, let your fatherhood give thanks for these things concerning my humble self.
For by God's grace I am still better off than my sins deserve, finding daily bread and a little rest.
And the worship of God's church is being carried out in an orderly, measured way—one, that is, which seems contrary to the course of the world.
So much so that even Satan could not tolerate the situation. Inflamed with his customary recklessness, he stirred up terrible and mighty things against us through sudden disturbances.

He arranged for us to celebrate a Passover resembling our Lord's Passover in every respect: on the very same day, at the very same hour, in the very same manner, and in the entire unfolding of events.
In place of Herod and Pilate, the leaders and rulers of our country; in place of the chief priests of the Jews and the authorities with them,
the heretics and the leading men among our people. In place of the guards and soldiers, in place of swords and clubs, those very swords and clubs.
In place of horns and shouting, those very horns and shouts. In place of Judas
the betrayer, the renowned and honored chief in [?]. While the Eucharist was still between his lips, he displayed a zeal greater than Judas's.
For he did not even wait for us to sing the hymn and go out to the Mount of Olives, as Judas himself had waited. Nor did he come against us with a kiss, as that man did,
but with a spear and a shield. Up to this point there was a resemblance to our Lord's Passover in every respect. But from this point onward, our Passover surpassed it.
That is, it surpassed our Lord's Passover in every respect—that bodily and sacramental Passover with Peter and his companions—because our Lord himself sent the twelve legions of angels,
whom he had then restrained from serving in their zeal by his words to Peter, openly now for the deliverance of our church.
And he wondrously accomplished deeds that shine forth to the glory of his power, deeds whose splendor a letter cannot contain an account of.
Perhaps even my unskilled tongue cannot sketch an outline of their wonderful nature through speech in person. Nevertheless, let them be kept for a meeting face to face
and for lengthy conversations, with God's help. But before I am granted this, let your fatherhood rejoice in what has happened, because it is truly glorious.
And always give thanks to our Lord on my behalf, because, through the greatness of his might, his enemies the heretics have submitted to him falsely, as it is written.
And when the Lord's blow broke the strength of their confidence, they turned to the barbarian rulers whom our sins had raised up over us.
And now they threaten me with death every day. I have shown them that it is very easy and even beneficial, although it is very frightening to them, because they have no hope.
Yet the Spirit of God, with her customary wonder-working, is gradually turning even the harshness of the barbarians toward peaceful relations with us.
And they are ashamed of them, just as they were ashamed of Assyria. And there is being returned
to the divine power, from the mouths of discerning people, the glory that befits it. So I ask your fatherhood to pray.
that I may be worthy of the grace of repentance and find mercy before our Lord, and spend the rest of my days living in a way that pleases God's will. The end.
40. To our father, holy in every way, His Holiness Mar Catholicos-Patriarch: your son Ishoʿyahb sends greetings in our Lord.
For me, O blessed [?] father, experience of what happened before has sufficiently persuaded me to be very forgiving of contempt,
in everything that adorns the ministry to which we have been called under the law of spiritual love. And I wanted, from now on, to withdraw from association with the wicked.
But your fatherly command, together with the entreaties of the honored men, compelled me to put those already tested to the test again.
For you thought—as it is also [?] to think—that people who have control over their own will can turn away from bad habits.
For this reason you both entreated and commanded, and I obeyed. But our shared hope did not bear fruit in the virtues that were called for.
For the persistence of bad habits was strengthened by an unchanging supply of support. They experienced the kindness of gentle authority and grew bold enough to show contempt without fear.

And now it is inevitable that some people should fall into these very same things, that some should be alarmed over these very same things, and that your kindness should suffer through these very same things.
For this reason I am informing your fatherly care briefly about things that are difficult to set out briefly.
For at this time two uncanonical bishops, Shemisho and Narsai, met with our humble [?] father, Mar
our metropolitan. Repaying him the debt of that uncanonical ordination which he had previously advanced to them, they joined him as he wished.
They found a certain man, an uneducated layman, as they themselves say, whose place of origin they did not know,
nor where he now lived, nor even his name, nor the conduct and habits in which he had been brought up, nor his work and occupation in the world,
nor to which ecclesiastical rank he belonged, nor whether he belonged at all to the pure church of the orthodox,
nor where he was coming from, nor where he was going.
So they gave this man, such as he was, the title of bishop and sent him off wherever he wished—according to them, to Adarbaigan.
[?] But in truth no one knows. Thus what has now happened has happened to put right what had previously happened so badly.
But I know that your fatherly care does not believe these things. And you do well not to accept them.
For it is very difficult to attribute senility and a lack of understanding of such actions to discerning people.
But if the Lord wills and I live, and we are granted an opportunity together to meet your fatherly care, I am ready to inform you, in their presence, of the full and exact truth of these matters,
from what we wrote to one another and what we said to one another face to face, before the event, at the time, and afterward.
Unless the present culmination, too, forestalls my efforts, as has been the pattern of events.
But before I am granted the opportunity to meet your kindness, pray for my weakness, that I may find mercy before our Lord. The end.
41. To our honored, God-loving brother, Mar Moses the priest. Ishoʿyahb sends greetings in our Lord.
Again, when the stirring of remembrance had puffed you up into your customary enthusiasm, you made use of my name as your subject even now.
And not long after the passing of years, you once again poured out a multitude of strange gifts in a letter and sent it to me.
Some of them were for Zaphenath-paneah, Rachel’s son, whoever he may be; others were for Jesse’s son, whoever he may be.
Still others were for Amram’s son, whoever he may be; and others also for Amittai’s son, whoever he may be. And since even these, apparently, were not enough for you,
from the comparison with the [?] of foolishness, you turned again toward the error of an imaginary future.
You depicted some imaginary catholicos—enough to bewilder the foolish [?] of a weak, senseless man, should he happen to be dazzled by such things.
Only after all this did you finally introduce the reason for the letter at its conclusion. Even this you clothed, amid many expressions of longing, in the appearance of profound need.
Thus, through the force of your persuasion, you gave a sluggish man a keen impulse to attend to your business.
For you have happened, I think, to repeat all these things in your letter to me

because you did not previously take the proper care in reading what I once wrote to you in reply to your letter to me. For I had already given you a little persuasion by means of a measured demonstration
of the properly ordered feelings that ought to move a free man who takes the spiritual law, understood spiritually—that is, the cause of [?]—as the subject of his letter.
Since, then, you did not read what was previously written about this, this is why it is so again now. Because
I too, however, am neglectful about writing further concerning these matters [?]. But I understood from what you wrote,
and also from what I learned from others, that the onslaught of a shortage of bread had reached you too—a shortage through which a prosperous people has endured upheaval and many changes.
It has reached the point that even the request now travels in the opposite direction: from those who have always had plenty to those who have been hungry for generations.
When I learned this, I felt the distress that I ought to feel. But I was not sufficiently able to support the need of someone brought low, as justice requires.
For, as you know, the whole worldly burden that brought you into unaccustomed need has also come upon us.
It struck us no little blow and has remained with us a long time, and we still lie beneath it. It has brought us back to our accustomed need through a multitude of demands that [?]
or cannot be met at all. Nevertheless, yielding a little to the spiritual law, a little to the appeal of the brothers’ need,
and a little also to the insistence of those who ask from the depths of deprivation, I took the little bread I possessed
and shared it as widely as possible: some in exchange for money, some as [?], and some also under worldly compulsion, according to the circumstances,
according to the person, and according to the produce of the villages. A portion of it has reached you too: bread as [?] for about ten days,
and bread in exchange for money for about twenty days. In measured quantity, it is three [?]; in terms of transport, it is a full load for your pack animal.
In the terminology of common use, it is thirty grivas. Divided by kind, it is ten of wheat and twenty of barley.
But in willingness and consent, I would have supplied your entire need, if I had been able. Receive, then, what has actually been done, such as it is.
And do not disregard the one who is willing, as though he did not exist. And if there should be [?] toward you from him, when [?] suffering, you will be to us as
is fitting for you. And if you act in these matters without being asked, [?] the grace of our Lord’s mercy.
Give thanks for his daily care for us. And pray for my lowliness, and remain well. End.
42. To our father, honored in every way, the holy Mar Cyriacus, metropolitan bishop. Ishoʿyahb: greetings in our Lord.
It is better for a man, our father, than other blessings to succeed in bringing a little peace to the church of God.
And better for the church of God than many other benefits is a little harmony among God’s guests, even if it is only a little, when it is rightly prompted by love.
For through the former—that is, the well-being of the church—the world’s continued existence is tended through the visitation of divine mercy.
And through [?]—that is, through priestly harmony—the continued celebration of God’s glory flourishes through the thanksgiving of eager tongues.
So now, too, the dignity of your fatherhood has graciously moved toward my humble lowliness, as though from a flower of exceptional potency, with the sweet fragrance of the praise of God,
who is called love by the whole world, and especially by the Scriptures of the Spirit, and indeed is love.
I do not know on what wings it flew, as though at rest—that is, effortlessly—and caught up the many who seek it through the power of its sweetness.
Some it turned toward customary discourse, and others toward thanksgiving for the distinction shown them.
Others, who are tried by adverse circumstances through the failure of their requests, it turned toward a better hope.
They found a means of help for their good desire: the celebrated freedom with which my lowliness approaches your fatherhood, which God arranged should be so filled with the perfect love
of your wisdom. And therefore, ahead of the many others who may perhaps be about to come,
if they should now learn of my lowliness’s success with your fatherhood, there came to me first, seeking your love,
the little children of your fatherhood, my brothers and the brothers of us all, who are on the eastern edge of your pasture and whose allotted fold is Balad.
They graze pleasantly on the edges of the wilderness and rest in innocence beside the waters of Eden, which flow from that branch that runs toward Assyria.
Many times things have turned out well for them. For at one time he granted an outstanding caretaker to the mother of cities, which is now administered through the care of your fatherhood:
namely, the admirable Paul, persuader of kings and champion of the word of truth.
And at another time, just recently—indeed, now, before our very eyes—he sent a distinguished adornment to the royal city and the patriarchal throne,
a man whose virtues even foreign mouths are compelled to proclaim.
And those whom I have described as having prospered in this way have now set their minds on the man beloved by us all, our honored brother Mar Marozan the bishop.
They asked that he should be their leader for the present. When their hope did not readily succeed in obtaining this arrangement, they lost heart and became distressed.
Then they found a hope—that is, the nearby one they have now found: because of the kindly love of your fatherhood toward me, they thought me capable of accomplishing this.
And they urged me with many pleas to appeal to your fatherhood. Some pleaded with me in person when they came, and all of them did so through a letter of appeal.

And when I was overcome by the fervor of my thoughts and put my trust in your fatherhood’s disposition toward me, I was eager to undertake this task in a son’s spirit: to appeal to your fatherhood as best I could, not
as I ought. For it would have been [?] for me personally to stand before you on this account and to do everything that the matter required.
But that is impossible, as is quite clear. I can only explain it to you in a letter, as time permits.
Therefore, honored father, I ask you: let this please your loving heart. Fulfill your sons’ request with a good conscience, and give relief also to my lowliness—not to say, honor me in this.
And do not be at all troubled about this, which everyone regards as good and praiseworthy. Divine choice has already preceded human choice.
And what [?] do we have to add of our own? Whether there is something divine in illness, as the physicians say,
or events are subject to human will, I think it is easy to hold to both.
For if your fatherhood, out of a noble conscience, questions whether to agree to such a thing, saying, “This man has acquired the dignity of a metropolitan,
and he ought not to be lowered by being placed in a lesser see,” the doubt is easily resolved from every angle.
To leave aside many other considerations, this alone is enough: his own consent does not diminish the man. Rather, he becomes greater when he desires lesser things.
Nor does granting the request diminish the one who grants it. Rather, it makes him greater when he answers the petition by granting what is asked.
Moreover, it is very fitting for your fatherhood’s dignity that fathers should become your sons, and that those who are metropolitans to others should be ranked among the little ones whom you teach.
But if it is not on this account, and instead the man’s unfitness [?] is put forward as the reason for refusing consent—for one of these reasons must be proposed—
how can we persuade the many peoples and renowned cities of this, when among them testimony to the man’s suitability is proclaimed in many languages?
But I also say this: even if this man is not as virtuous as everyone who knows him says,
but is in fact otherwise before God, while he is well regarded by people—and this to such an extent that everyone who knows him calls him [?]—
a shortcoming of this kind does people no harm, since it is entirely hidden from them.
For I do not think it is easy for all these people now to think ill of someone whose uprightness they have already seen attested through many trials.
And if, again, it is not things like these, but shortcomings [?] of the kind found in us all,
that your fatherhood’s refusal has in view, preventing this appointment, then who indeed will escape danger?
Who can say, “You are pure, my heart, and I have been cleansed of sins”? Or whose confidence is not secretly struck down by the consciousness of his sins?
But I truly consider myself unworthy of either heaven or earth. Nor have I ever washed my hands in innocence
and walked around the Lord’s altar. Indeed, I already acknowledge that I am unworthy even of divine mercy.
I am a miserable human being, brought low by passions. Yet I am greatly sustained by God’s grace.
Yet God's church also looks on me with a compassionate eye. Neither virtuous people nor those godly men despise my lowliness.
For every wise mind knows how to bear the shortcomings of others by considering its own.
And so we must all live together with one another and with God's church. And I believe, honored father, that since you can understand more than these things,
you are obliged to put matters right even more than those who understand them. It is therefore neither advantageous nor
beneficial for the matter to turn from an insistent appeal into an apparent cause of stumbling. For it certainly can be distorted, especially by hasty tongues.
And immediately they give the matter an odious name, namely envy. They disturb you, us, and the entire community's thinking.
Perhaps the scandal may even spread beyond the boundaries of the church. And who can live with that?
Or who would not be distressed enough to breathe his last every day, if he has a conscience that is stirred by disgrace? Yes, my father, let me find mercy before you.
Accept my humble appeal with the [?] of fathers. Through the power of your wisdom, arrange an excellent conclusion to the matter at hand.
Satisfy your sons' longing in their worthy request, and attend to your lowly neighbor with support that brings benefit.
Grant my lowliness, too, the encouragement of having my appeal accepted, so that perhaps, in matters yet to arise, I may rely on my present freedom to speak and approach with confidence.
And when, with God's help, I discern rightly, I may also help others through your fatherhood and increase the honor of your fatherhood among others.
And act before the forthcoming [?] in this present matter. For the man who was twice entrusted with the care of the two metropolitan cities
can certainly guide this small and peaceful flock without stumbling, by God's grace and with the help of your fatherhood.

Thus, through him, honor may increase, and God's church may receive the order appropriate to it. For my lowliness and for those encouraged toward what is good, may there be increasing cause for thanksgiving to God's glory.
May he, in his mercy, make the honor of your fatherhood shine in his church throughout all the days of your life. Amen. Finished.
43. To the true believer, who falls little short of the glory befitting him, our honored and distinguished chief, Mar Yazdhan. Ishoʿyahb: greetings in our Lord.
That neither deliberate initiative nor the course of everyday affairs has brought my humble self—or rather, your greatness—
into contact with one another, even if only through written lines, for this long time, is already clear both to you and to me, and also to those who are concerned about this.
While I absolve you of such blame, for reasons that are clear, I place myself under a burden of guilt that makes me sigh.
For it was fitting that, from the time when the aberration of that hostile opinion pressed upon your honor from God's priests,
until the harm reached the point of danger, to our sorrow and the grief of the Lord's whole church,
I too, weak as I am, should have run with a willing spirit after the one helping you, and poured a little water for washing.
If the matter was one of healing, I should have been assigned a place among the attendants. And if the work was to involve persuasion, understanding, and united assistance,
even then I should not have excluded myself from the number of those concerned for your honor, your good name, and the increase of your virtues.
But now, because of the adversities that pressed upon me, and the relentless upheaval of distressing changes,
and the great affliction that plunged the whole world into the depths of despair, I too was prevented from doing what I was obliged to do.
Suddenly, amid the personal sorrows that Satan stirred up against me through the servants of his will—the heretics, the enemies of God—
your loving letter came upon me, breathing out the sweet fragrance of love for the true faith.
You bestowed encouragement in the struggle upon me, weak and fainthearted as I am. Indeed, zeal for the faith and love for orthodoxy are fitting for you from every quarter:
from your father, for one, whose faith, I think, fell little short of that of Peter and Abraham;
and from your mother, who likewise fell little short of the measure of her husband's great faith;
and again from yourself, since you already possess a power of understanding sufficient to examine matters like these.
You therefore did well to come promptly to my aid in the struggle that Satan brought upon me through the wicked people who serve his schemes.
May your strength therefore increase, Basil, with God's help strengthening you. Add greater efforts each day until the excellent completion,
which moves all who fear God everywhere to give thanks to God.
But so that, when I recount the nature of the events—that is, the insolence of the wicked, the beginning of the outbreak of their madness, and the things they subsequently dared to do—
and how they now stir up constant turmoil by agitating the authorities and the people of the region every day,
and what I myself, under pressure, decided to do, whether by going to the authorities or by sending a delegation to them, and record all such things in a letter,
it may not grow excessively long, I have now sent to you our honored brother, Mar Hnanisho, the abbot, to inform you about everything,
so that you may hear from him what is needed, and may yourself do what is needed. After this, I ask you, by the mercies of God,
not to turn the conduct of your life toward anything that appears contrary to the fear of our Lord. Do not give the enemies
of the Lord an opportunity to place a stain upon your honor, as upon an honored member of our Lord's body.
Let the wound of your transgression not become a heartbreak, with the enemies' abuse planted in it every day like a tormenting thorn.
Yes, my brother, comfort my affection for you in Christ. Turn toward your conscience with heartfelt concern. Look a little at what is near, and consider a little what is far away.
Let your father in the flesh be your example in virtue, whose great faith God demonstrated through his very deeds.
The memory of his zeal in the fear of God is celebrated on the lips of many.
Why, then, as in his case, are the bare feet of God's priests not constantly present in the courtyards of your house?
And why is your table not sanctified every day by the faithful blessings of our Lord's holy ones?
And why is priestly service not continually performed in your dwelling through the pure prayers of the Lord's ministers?
And, to speak still more forcefully: Why are all those everywhere who need correction and despise their duty not directed and brought to order through you and by you?
For your eyes and the eyes of all of us have seen all such qualities of dutifulness and fear of our Lord
in that blessed man whose nature, household, and honor you have inherited. And all grace comes from the Lord.
But what comes from you, I do not know. I therefore ask you, my brother: remember the grace of our Lord.
Remember the afflictions that brought you close to death, which many times brought you back, against all hope, from the depths of [?] to life.
Remember every danger from the sufferings that can torment our short lives [?] with changing afflictions and replace natural death with the bitterness of adversity.
Remember, then, that we are dust, and our days on earth are like vapor. We are like water poured out on the ground that cannot be gathered up.
I know, my brother, I know that you are a hardhearted man, a person lacking in fear, and that you feel little in your sufferings.
As a result, you also come to disregard sins just as you disregard those who correct you. As it is written: “Without fear and without denial, sins are strengthened.”
Who, then, is Paul? Or who is Apollos, that you are angry with them? Are those who proclaim the truth to you enemies? Or, like
wicked men, do they rob you by deceit? Is he not the one who raised you—or rather your childhood companion—who has always been the priest of your city?
Or has he not rightly maintained an undying love for you and your father's entire household?
Or did you not long ago lay obligations of kindness upon him, his people, and his dwelling?
Was he perhaps obliged to repay you evil for good? But anyone who does so is cursed by Scripture. And it would indeed have been repaying evil
if he had neglected and given up correcting you at a time when the stumbling block of your arrogance had spilled over even onto our Lord's church.
And he would have been an enemy if he had not expended all the strength he could muster in the struggle to correct you.
But now that he has done as he ought and fulfilled the spiritual law with human love, should he be considered your enemy because he proclaimed the truth to you?
But perhaps you say, “I have been wrongfully accused, and I am innocent in my own eyes and before God.” Very well.
Why, then, do you not openly establish your innocence to the conscience of your beloved priest and to all our Lord's holy ones?
For this is what they all seek and pray to achieve: namely, to have you free from blame.
But if your conscience is not clear before God in the matter for which his priests accuse you, why, then, are you angry with the priests?
Or why do you despise your own correction? Or why do you set yourself against
those who correct you? Do you think you are harming them by this? It is obvious where the harm falls. But if it is not that,
nor this either, but rather, with a shaken conscience covered by the darkness of insensitivity, you perhaps despise and act blindly,
and you scorn and disdain the life-giving [?] of Christian conduct and the humble [?] that follow them:
Know, then, that you need the many prayers of the saints if, God forbid, you should incline toward this downfall.
May God not allow it to happen! May the suffering of your turning aside and the evil of your defeat not bring grief to our people and joy to our enemies.
May those who hate you not say, “Aha! Aha! Our eyes have seen it happen to him!” Rather, may the Lord save; may the Lord deliver.
May the Lord help. May the Lord have mercy. May the Lord show compassion. May the Lord turn toward you. May the Lord visit you. May the Lord [?] from the dust of sins,
and raise you from the ashes of passions. May the Lord give you a new heart and a new spirit. May the Lord give strength and power to his servant. Blessed is God.
Be constant in prayer, and do not let the Lord’s worship pass you by. Receive the reading of the spiritual Scriptures with the delight that comes from discernment.
Whenever the divine mysteries are consecrated, throw yourself face down on the ground. Feel sorrow and shed tears.
Make the tax collector’s cry your own, often and without ceasing, saying, “God, have mercy on me, a sinner.”
When your heart has been softened by the sighs of prayer, call upon the Lord, and he will open the eyes of your understanding, so that you may know your condition and what you ought to do.
When you know, take care to set yourself right. When you have set yourself right, love those who have been concerned about you.
When you love them, honor them as God’s guests and rejoice with them. Sharing their joy, join them in praising
God, who [?] you. Give my humble self also, and the whole holy Church, a reason for praise and thanksgiving, to the glory of the merciful God,
who desires that all people should be saved and turn to the knowledge of the truth and to a life of righteousness.
May he, in his compassion, strengthen you to do his will at all times, all the days of your life. Amen. It is finished.
44. To our father, honored in every way, the holy Mar Gabriel, bishop and metropolitan. Ishoʿyahb sends greetings in our Lord.
That the lot of his sins has fallen to me to live beside Satan’s nest, our father, where in every season he hatches the offspring of vipers
and obtains from them destructive scourges to destroy the lives of all people—you yourself already know, since this is something evident to everyone.
But how, whenever they encounter the world’s turmoil and misery, they are nourished and strengthened as though by an unhealthy condition of the air,
and swiftly dart forward to wound weak human beings—these things we alone can perceive beforehand and recognize, we who, according to God’s word to the prophet,
have been allotted a dwelling among scorpions, or rather in the nest of vipers, as I have said.
For this reason, the evil news of the wicked people’s deeds, which I see from a nearby lookout, must be proclaimed far away,
so that everyone may be moved to take precautions for his life, as far as his strength allows. The very end has therefore come upon the world, our God-loving father, as you know.
Already the rebellion foretold by the Spirit of God has come and taken hold everywhere—the rebellion that must occur with Satan’s revelation. Or perhaps
it is near; or rather, it has already begun to be fulfilled in practice, that saying: “When the Son of Man comes, will he indeed find faith on the earth?”
And to leave aside the many other things about which I, perhaps because of faintheartedness, think with such weakness.
I am briefly informing Your Holiness of this one matter, about which I was also compelled to write: those wicked men and blasphemers who are the subject here.
The surge of their madness carried them away with a demonic expectation, and they found a favorable time for their success, for reasons that are evident.
First, the readiness of the present rulers to listen to those who approach them with the whispers of silver
and gilded arguments. Second, the great number of wicked supporters who formerly belonged to their heresy
but are now numbered among those in power. Third, the acceptance and success that the people of Tikrit enjoy before the leaders and rulers there.
Fourth, along with these things, the activity of Satan, which is at work in the children of disobedience, who do not persevere in the love of the truth by which they might live.
So they went as they did and approached as they were accustomed to do. Although they spoke no word of wisdom
and presented no intelligent argument, nor gave any demonstration that they belonged to our Lord,
and were entirely unable to do anything appropriate to an audience before reasonable rulers,
they obtained the fulfillment of their desire and returned to trouble us. They also found a ruler, [?], who gave them his full support.
They went down to the dung heap in front of our city gate, just as they themselves are the dung of the church.
They built themselves a house of ridicule and contempt under the name of a church, close to the gathering place of all those who, to relieve themselves, are, as
usual, obliged to go there. From there they also stir up causes for disturbances every day.
This happens especially through the constant blasphemies that they utter every day against the church of God with their insolent mouths. And those who are held in honor among our people
are the longstanding offspring of their heresy. They are loyal to them and belong to them both by nature and by choice.
The one who, among them all, is regarded as the foremost, and whom circumstances also favor abundantly, had an orthodox Christian father
and a heretical Christian mother. He began with his mother's faith and moved a little toward his father's,
but after these things he was carried away again into outright paganism, the open paganism of robbers. Afterward, along with paganism, he also entered the appalling fellowship of heretics.
When he was constrained by public disgrace, as though by a blow from his conscience, he turned for a little while toward the church of God,
until he recovered from his fear of death and his dread of the rulers. Now once again, like a dog returning to its vomit, to the root of bitterness from which he sprang through his mother,
he has returned in a rush of madness. For those who promote wickedness, he is a dependable supporter and one who fulfills the things they boast about.
For this reason they exalt themselves and grow arrogant and are difficult to endure, as it is written: “I saw the wicked boasting and rising high like the trees of the forest.”
Our own people, however, are poor in strength and lacking in wealth, and entirely deprived of worldly influence and connections.
Nevertheless, with God's help, they possess zeal for the true faith.
They groan deeply and are distressed at the evil sight of the filthy sign that Satan has placed at the gate of their city.
Often they are also inflamed by an impetuous rush to risk death in matters that run contrary to the times.
Yet it seemed helpful to me to calm the faith-loving people, through the customary admonition, from the violent impulses of their agitation,
and to present myself before the authorities of the time, although I bear a bodily illness not much less severe than the suffering and distress of my soul.
And now, with God's help, I have begun my journey, knowing that I must stand in the midst of Tikrit as though in an arena of wicked men.
For besides Kabab [?], who may perhaps be there in person, there are also many of his associates
who are my opponents and supporters of the wicked. Yet it lies in God's hands, as it is written, to make all grace abound among his servants.
For even if, because of the unworthiness of my weakness, he should choose to allow his truth, as expressed through us, to be despised beneath the arrogance of its persecutors,
even then this little labor for the word of his truth is not without benefit to me, a sinner. Thanks be to him for his mercy toward me in everything.
But if he should do what is better and grant the truth of his faith the glory that befits it at this time,
which is, indeed, a time when the world has been abandoned, then through the peace of many I will henceforth increase my thanksgiving, to the praise of his name at all times.
If, then, you, our honored father, can offer to the wisdom of your fatherhood, or to the zeal of that Christ-loving people,
whose growth in faith has been nourished by the dew of God's grace, some assistance through thoughtful counsel,
or a journey involving bodily exertion, or anything that appears useful for this impending struggle,
act diligently, as befits your preeminent excellence, in everything that brings distinction to the beauty of Christians with the glory that befits it.
But if the times, with their adversities, have hindered you from such things, take special care for us in the church of God,
and pray for us with humble hearts, that God may open a door for our message, so that we may render to the truth of his faith the praise it deserves,
and that we may return in peace to the ministry that called us, without disturbance or conflict with wicked men. And so that you may know our situation and what they have planned to do,
I have now sent you our honored brother, Mar Hnanisho, the abbot. Receive him, then, in the Lord, as you customarily do,
and send him on his way in peace and without delay, so that he may soon come to me, wherever the merciful God may graciously choose to direct us.
Through your fatherhood, let the greetings of my lowliness be conveyed to all the children of your fatherhood, my beloved brothers and those of the whole community.
And pray for me, that I may spend the remainder of my days living in a manner pleasing to God's will. End.
45. To the lovers of God, my beloved brothers, the chaste clergy and the faithful people in the city of Balad: Isho'yahb sends greetings in our Lord.
I have read what you wrote to me, my brothers, and have thanked our Lord for your diligence in the fear of God.
Yet I was greatly seized by bewilderment and doubt when I unexpectedly encountered the news of what had happened.
For it seems that there is no limit to the expense of your present effort to acquire a spiritual guardian for yourselves at a time when the world is given over to neglect.
Yet the simplicity of the undertaking is also without limit in matters that maintain the traditional order derived from ancient laws. In the former case, the inquiry extends to simplicity.
But in this case it extends to the simplicity of obedience throughout the whole community—that is, obedience to the community’s leaders. Therefore, my dear friends, until the outcome
of these matters, the zeal of your love brings me joy and anxiety together. For I do not yet know
how the heads of ecclesiastical administration—that is, the administrators of the community—will rightly judge what has now newly taken place at your hands.
For this is truly something new. How was it devised by the local people? Or who persuaded them that something never tried among us was possible?
Or how did such a meeting come about between them: a city needing a bishop, and a bishop needing a city;
a people agreeing upon a man, and a man finding rest among the people? And all this to the point that they should rush eagerly toward one another.
For anyone considering these things is swept into uncertainty of thought until the events reveal themselves—that is, until the final outcome, as I said.
The matter therefore deserves caution in every respect, so that the people may not regret what they have done, nor the man suffer because of his obedience.
Nor should the metropolitan become excessively agitated, either troubling anyone or being troubled by what has happened.
Nor should news of what you have done be carried by others to our father, the lord patriarch, with a distorted interpretation.
Rather, diligently give everyone what is owed to him: honor to whom honor is owed, and love to whom love is owed,
obedience to whom obedience is owed, and an appeal to whom an appeal is owed; and, before anything else, give our father, the lord patriarch, information about what has happened.
The questions surrounding the undertaking, as well as its commendable features, are certainly known. To put it briefly, they are these: the bishop you have chosen is worthy.
Worthy too are the people who chose him. Commendable is the unanimity of the election, confirmed by all the people, and by outsiders along with the people. Commendable also is
the zeal of your eagerness, because you did not neglect to [?] a spiritual guardian for yourselves at this time when duty has been neglected by many.
Commendable too is the great effort you have made in your appeals to the metropolitan, or in the [?] directed toward those who plead with him.
For it is not fitting, as I believe, my brothers, that in your eager haste you should seize matters of this kind into your own authority.

Nor is it fitting for anyone, out of simplicity—that is, love of what is good—to disregard the ecclesiastical order that has proceeded according to the canons through traditions handed down from ancient times
and requires proper agreement from all the ranks of the Church. Therefore, brothers, if you consider it easy to heal
the offense that such impropriety has caused, or is causing, the fathers of the community, diligently and without neglect do whatever seems beneficial to you.
For [?], you had already considered these matters before you even began to act. Bring them to completion as you intended.
May our Lord open before you everywhere the door of his peace, and strengthen you through the spirit of his wisdom to heal the wounds that need this.
And may the strength of your appeal, with God’s help, bring into harmony, agreement, and love with you
your metropolitan and all the fathers of the community; and may the episcopal throne of your city be established in its rightful order.
And may the beloved priest whom you have chosen sit upon it in truth, in the tabernacle of the Lord. And may the Lord’s gracious Spirit guide him on the path of life.
To investigate justice, to advance righteousness, and to show holy compassion toward the people’s sins for many years.
May the Lord rejoice in his deeds, and may the soul of the people delight in him. May his strength increase in good things, and may the people prosper through his prayer.
May the peace of your city flourish, and may loving concord increase among all the orders of your church. And may God’s helping right hand protect you
from every harm each day. May you be strengthened and sanctified to keep his commandments at all times, all the days of your lives. Amen. It is finished.
This is how it seems to me, brother, and it is pleasing to all who fear God; perhaps you too approve:
It is right to write to you only in this way: To our chaste and God-loving, honored brother, Mar So-and-so. Ishoyahb: greetings in [?].
I beg you, brother, desist from this toil that lies upon you, and keep yourself out of everyone’s mouth.
Rather, serve God with a humble spirit, taking care to maintain that helpful quietness which all the saints praise.
Pray for the tranquility of the world and the peace of the holy church. Pray also for me, that I may spend the remainder of my days living in a way pleasing to God’s will.
But as the time demands, the occasion calls for, and your holiness has undertaken to bear, perhaps it is necessary to write in this way:

To him who has sanctified his bodily senses through spiritual labors, so that through him the light of hidden things might shine upon the dark world, and who spiritually provides help for all with the bright lamp of his understanding;

who, from the [?] of his lips, extends glorious deliverance to every soul in every time of distress, and fills the weary hearts of needy people with the nourishment of peace and the sweetness of rest;
and who imitates in everything the one whom the saving word appointed as a model for the perfect: a true consecrated man and a scrupulous ascetic,
a perfect model of spiritual conduct, our honored master, Mar So-and-so. Ishoyahb the sinner, least of all and weakest of all, bearing the name and serving
in the office with a troubled conscience, needing mercy at every moment to find hope of compassion from the Lord of all, in our Lord himself, the fountain of peace:
May peace increase for you at every moment. For the conscience of many is sufficient to attest that the beauty of deeds is far superior to praise in words, O you who excel in praiseworthy things,
since help comes no less from success in them than from inability itself.
In this case, as far as the [?] of need; in that case, as far as the testimony of the mind.
And therefore I did not consider it necessary that, amid those very praises, we should feel [?] from fears.
For we suffer—how could we not?—if poverty of persuasion should strike down even the pride of promises, especially in someone who, even in the apparent beauty within,
already sees the measure of his own littleness. Therefore, chaste man, let the praise that comes from God suffice for the praiseworthy qualities of your honored person,
with the testimony of the whole world accompanying it. But concerning the one matter on which I have been persuaded to appeal to you, I now make my appeal.
For you know that I have been appointed to be a servant and minister to these poor people of Nineveh.
And for all the adverse afflictions that press upon them, I am called upon to provide relief.
They used to cry out along with all the others: “A good caretaker and a wise helper, the honorable Mar So-and-so!” Because of him they lived in great peace.
And through his efforts many improvements came to our country, especially to the churches and monasteries and to our entire order.
As you yourself know particularly well. But the times envied our tranquility and snatched this helpful man away from us.
And we face suffering amid great dangers, if God [?], just as we have already begun to endure.

For this reason I appeal to you, as though through this poor people to whose service I have been appointed, to write about these matters to the holder of authority and administrator of public affairs.
Ask that they return this man, So-and-so, to us. You have the power to help us if you wish, and this request of yours will be granted without hindrance, to the relief of us all.

And together with us, our entire region will benefit. Therefore, lover of God, do not withhold the gift of help from the poor people who have called upon you. Rather, visit us as you customarily do, and assist the weak who remain silent.
And add to your letter about this matter persuasive force sufficient to bring the petition of the weak to a helpful conclusion. Bring us this man as governor, as though from your own side.
By doing this, you will secure a peaceful life for us, and especially for the churches and monasteries and all the holy people within them.

Then, being able to fulfill their service for everyone through their customary prayer without disturbance, they will assist you in the struggle for the peace of the world, to the praise of the Lord’s name.
May he, by his grace, make your well-being flourish in the church, to the glory of his worshipers. Amen. The end.
47. To our father, honored in every way, the holy Mar Cyriacus, bishop and metropolitan: Ishoyahb sends greetings in our Lord.
I joyfully received the letter of your love, our God-loving father, and thanked our Lord for your health.
But the fact that you have been so deeply shaken by the repeated upheaval of distressing changes has also caused me great pain.
For a little earlier I had already begun to suspect this suffering from the availability [?] of essential supplies:
Those supplies which, from the bounty of your land, used to give the inhabitants of your city an abundance of enjoyment. With little hope, I was anxious about

these matters: whether the pressure of want had suddenly fallen upon the priestly people, and whether, through the onslaught of the trials that had beset them, the unfortunate people had lost the abundance of their livelihood.
And whether the distress of Nisibis had brought to the [?] of Assyria those delicacies for the pampered stomach with which the markets of Nisibis used daily to arouse the appetite of the freeborn.
And whether something had indeed happened that would have seemed unbelievable: that a renowned city, abundantly supplied with every good thing and sustaining many thousands of people,
