should turn to the hungry farmer who remained after the devastation of Assyria, to find relief for its needy in a time of hardship.
While I was thus caught up in such shifting thoughts, not long afterward I also received the letter of your fatherhood.
Reading it changed my uncertainty about the suffering into sorrow beyond doubt. From then on I continued mourning your sufferings,
amid sufferings that are certainly in store for us too. And I quote, as appropriate to the occasion, what was spoken by the holy and life-giving mouth:
“If these things happened to the green wood, what then will happen to us, who are dry wood both by nature and by our own choice?”
Thanks also, then, to the mercy of our Lord, both on account of these things and for these things.

I therefore beg Your Fatherhood to pray that we may indeed have a conscience worthy of the patience of God's kindness toward us, so that [?], from all his blessings and also from discipline itself, he may grant us fruits of eternal life.
May we all be found worthy of them through the mercies of [?] of our God. Amen. As for that matter which your love took as the subject of your letter to me,
I wished to bring it to an excellent fulfillment with a cheerful conscience. But the longing of my mind was hindered by
the weakness of the capacity that serves bodily affairs, as regards the times, as regards the household, and as regards
our circumstances. In accordance with my ability and intention, I have sent Your Fatherhood a thousand kors of barley; but in actual measure and quantity,
a hundred grivas, as you wrote to me. And if we should happen to need them shortly afterward, you will be able to give us the principal and [?], with an addition and a surplus.
But if God's grace keeps us above such needs, the great church of Nisibis will owe us
a thousand kors of barley forever. And, mixing still more cheerfulness with sorrow, I say:
I searched all my treasuries and all my chests to find some object or deed suitable for repaying that dignified greeting sent from your [?] to my lowliness, and I found nothing.
As it is said where it is said. For the fruits of our field and the produce of our river bring wealth of this kind into our dwellings:
namely, poverty. However, a few days ago the command of our Lord's will rained down upon us a few dates from the lower country,
and I have sent them to Your Fatherhood as a lavish offering whose greatness you cannot do justice to. They are a great number,
not much less than one small measure full. May Your Fatherhood therefore receive them as befits the deed, and pray for me. It is finished.
48. To the weak sons of genuine believers and true Christians.
Qamisho, Sanya, Babusa, [?], Isaac, Bar Sahda, and Dadizd. Ishoʿyahb, a stranger who by God's grace serves the church
that is holy in Nineveh: may peace abound to you in God Almighty. Very fitting for the downfall of the world and the shattering of human lives is
the evil of faithlessness, which it has now fallen to you alone to suffer before the rest of the lost, you poor people.
For already there has been fulfilled in you what our Lord said about the present times: “When the Son of Man comes, will he find faith on earth?”
For now, through the evidence of your deeds, you cry out as though aloud, in answer to the uncertainty in our Lord's saying: “No, there is no faith among us.”
How so? I heard about it before and did not want to believe it. Then I heard it again and was compelled to accept it without doubt:
a demon flew to you, one of those who rebel on Mount Alfaf, and buzzed like a fierce hornet at the door of the room
on which you had bestowed the honored name of the holy church in the fortress of Beth Babai. He placed the seals of his incantations on it and departed,
while all of you were rolling about there like lifeless stones. Your mouths were closed to speech,
and your limbs were withered and unable to act. Not one of you was found who moved his hand even as far as the space between his eyes.
And he made the sign of the cross over his face, that is, over his heart, so that God's help might come to you.
And you might have been able to wake from the sleep of mental blindness and see into what degradation, contempt, mockery, and ridicule Satan has brought you,
through a single unclean raven, the servant of his assault. But you remained, as people say, motionless, unfeeling, and insensible, like
mute idols. You could not even bring the holy mysteries out of there, even as weak people might,
who, despite their weakness, show extraordinary concern over any pressing matter in their affairs.
Instead, like people without hope and without God in the world, you abandoned even the holy and life-giving mysteries inside the seal of demons.
And you all moved away to the dwelling places of your sins, with a shame you did not even feel.
Who, then, can now weep over you as you deserve? Or who is capable of binding up the wound of your downfall with the bandage of prayer?
Or how could anyone who still retains a Christian understanding not consider you miserable and deserving of heartfelt lamentation?
Believe me, you poor, sleeping men—if you understand what is being said, and if Satan has not utterly destroyed all your capacity for discernment—
that this demonstration of your faith, that is, your faithlessness and your indifference toward this deed deserving of astonishment and condemnation,
seems to me to be the beginning of the downfall of the many who, at the time of Satan's coming into the world,
will lose themselves by abandoning faith in the truth of the sure hope, through all the deception of unrighteousness that takes place among those who are perishing, as it is written.
I groan deeply and am bewildered, and I am brought down into the depths of despondency,
especially when I consider where and among whom the stumbling block of sin began to appear.
That is, among you! Some of you are the biological sons of blessed bishops,
while others are the true heirs of genuine believers and the well-trained pupils of respected priests.
And now, through the laxity of your will, you have destroyed your fathers' entire good reputation. If it were possible for him to awaken
now from the sleep of death—the blessed Bishop Simeon, in whose days these weeds, the heretics, sprang up in Christ's field in this region,
and who waged great struggles against them, even to bloodshed and death, until he handed over his struggle, his episcopal seat, his office, his house, and his inheritance to his natural heir—
and if he were to come now and see his children's children, some offering their sons and daughters as a sacrifice to the heretics, Satan's servants,
and others despising the things Christians hold precious, like people who have lost their minds,
and becoming partners and companions of the heretics, welcoming, honoring, praising, and comforting those at whose hands he himself endured trials,
what would he think and feel? With what cries would he lament his weak children, who have renounced the good inheritance of his faith
and submitted to the heretics? But the expression of his suffering is plain to those with discernment, even though that priestly mouth is now silent.
from the rebuke suited to the folly of his sons. For [?] will rebuke at the proper time before the fearful judgment seat of Christ our Lord.
So too the blessed bishop Qamisho, who abolished idol worship among the people of Sin through his diligent labors,
passed on the good inheritance of the true faith to his disciples and to his own bodily children.
So too all the faithful fathers of each one of you, who departed from bodily life with a good name and pure faith,
left you an inheritance of their faith, their possessions, their honor, their authority, and their leadership.
And perhaps, having also strengthened their hopes for you before God, the Lord of all, with the weapon of prayer, behold, there is preserved among you
through God's help and through the faith and prayer of your fathers, all the honor, leadership, and authority of your country at this time.
So that you cannot find in any pretext an escape or relief for the slackness and negligence in which you live.
Rather, when God's judgment against you is set in motion at the proper time, everyone will acknowledge God's justice, for his judgments are entirely upright.
Therefore I, O weak people, since I suppose that, because of the great contempt in which you persist, you may even be reluctant to read the letter,
and perhaps will not even tolerate someone else reading it before you—for this reason I am reluctant to write to you about this matter at the length it deserves.
I also think, however, that your situation at this time needs prayer more than a letter. And before judgment, may God visit you with the mercies of his grace.
And I too, sinful and miserable, [?] toward you, to see whether the good hope of your fathers' faith is preserved, and whether you are at all concerned about what has happened or not.
In short, to see whether you have not entirely lost Christian goodness, I wished to test you in this matter, even if others think differently.
Until you take upon your hearts, your tongues, and your hands zeal for the faith of our Lord,
and break the unclean seals that Satan, through the servant of his will, placed on the door of your church,
and show it the care it deserves, rebuilding it, enlarging it, providing it with priestly ministry, and consecrating it as befits God's church,
you are not permitted, by the word of our Lord, to enter any church anywhere or to share in the divine mysteries. And if
you happen, while making false excuses, to say—or the heretics mislead you into thinking—that what happened took place by order of the [?], this is not true at all.
For the Hagarene Arabs do not help those who attribute suffering and death to God, the Lord of all. And if they have happened to help them for some reason,
you can nevertheless inform the Hagarenes and persuade them about this matter, if you give it the attention you ought.
Therefore, my brothers, act wisely in everything. Give Caesar what belongs to Caesar, and God what belongs to God.
And may the exalted God himself, in whose hands is every grace with which to benefit those who fear him,
make you perfect in every good work, to do his will at every moment, all the days of your lives. Amen. It is finished.
49. To our father, honored in every way, Mar Gabriel, metropolitan bishop. Ishoʿyahb: greetings in our Lord.
A little while ago, our father, when we were shaken by the assault of the wicked,
we hastily turned our thoughts toward you, as toward steadfast guardians of orthodoxy.
We wrote and informed you, with faithful confidence, of what the circumstances then permitted us to do and what we were prepared to do. Not long after these disturbances,
but at the very beginning of our departure, the mercy of God's grace suddenly came upon us with a wonder beyond words and drove the assault of the wicked away from us.
It drove some of them far away and others into the recesses of their hiding places. And with equal amazement,

it turned us toward thanksgiving and the peace to which we were accustomed. Not only that: we also hope that the demonstration of our Lord's power will grow stronger, to bring down the wicked man's insolence from its arrogance within a short time,
as they have already begun to feel. Let your fatherhood therefore rejoice in these things and duly thank our Lord for them.
Pray also about what is yet to come, that by God's grace these things may reach an excellent conclusion, for the glory of the holy Church and the joy of the faithful.
I also thought it right to send you, together with this letter, the letter that I wrote to your holiness a little while ago from the midst of the storm of afflictions,
so that you may know more fully the aggression of Satan's servants and the wonderful working of God's power,
and the swift change that suddenly came to us from that incomprehensible mercy. As you learn more fully, you will marvel; and as you marvel, you will give thanks and praise.
Along with all this, pray also for my weakness, that I may spend the remainder of my days living in a way that pleases God's will. End.
60. To the lovers of God, my dear brothers John, priest and archdeacon, and Ta'i, head of the [?] of Erbil, and all those with them who wrote to me: Ishoyahb sends greetings in our Lord.
I received and read what you wrote to me, and I thanked our Lord for your concern, inspired by love of what is good, and for the demonstration of your love toward my humble self.
Nevertheless, the conscience of my humble self does not agree with the things that you have judged advantageous.
For on what reasonable grounds, if one considers carefully, could there be any benefit at this time
in such a move? A person is moved to change his [?] either by the hope of spiritual benefits,
or by a desire for bodily life and the other things that adorn human existence with greater prosperity.
Worshiping the grace of our Lord, I acknowledge that I have a moderate measure of these things here. God's providence has not left my humble self
to be tormented by the hope of greater worldly advantages—those, that is, which are to be found in other places.
For someone to abandon the fervor of his labor and the measured arrangements established through prolonged care,
to change good habits acquired with difficulty, and to abandon steadfastness in the continual struggle against heretics and pagans,
and the fruit gathered from these things for the benefit of spiritual life, together with the other things that accompany them in good practices,
and to move away to settle among things inferior to these is not, in my opinion, the action of someone with sound judgment.
For an empty title brings people no benefit. It is therefore good for everyone to remain in the calling to which he was called.
While striving for the things that please our Lord, that is enough for him. Yet, as helpers of your joy, if you ask [?] for advice:
I can point out to you someone suitable for the ministry of your church and for leadership of the community, if the Lord wills.
For by God's grace there are people suitable for this, although they are very reluctant; and the Lord knows those who are his.

In his grace he visits his church with a suitable leader and grants our whole community the gift of his help. Therefore, my beloved brothers, apply yourselves diligently to the services of your festival.
Turn your hopeful expectation toward God's mercy, so that in his compassion he may attend to you in every matter, keep you [?] free from blame, and supply
what you lack through the mercy of his grace. Pray also for my lowly self, that I may spend the rest of my days living in a way that pleases God's will. End.

51. To the holy men of our Lord and my fathers, Mar Habib, Mar Zuzoy, Mar Narsai, Mar Marammeh, and those with them who wrote to me. Ishoʿyahb, the common son of your fatherly love: greetings in our Lord.
I received and read what you wrote to me, and I thanked our Lord for your well-being.
And if I say to you what was said, 'I thought he would surely come out to me, stand and call on the name of the Lord,
and wave his hand over the place, and it would be healed of the affliction,' what, then, will you say to me, as that man's servants said to him?
Or how will you rebuke my lack of faith, as the prophet's miracle rebuked Naaman?
For the nature of my situation required both the scrutiny of rational thought and persuasive power like that.
And if you possess this—that is, power [?]—give thanks for our Lord's gift. But if, according to my own worldly thinking and that of others like me,
you had not yet reached the state of perfection, since you had not first seen the exact circumstances of the matters at issue.
For it is very easy to make a judgment from a distance when we look only at the outward appearance of a matter.
That is why there are also many who give the advice you have given. When they approach an examination of the matters at issue, they persist in their assertion without offering proof,
saying only, 'This seems to be beneficial'—that is, precisely what seems so to you as well.
Therefore, blessed men, provide either the power to accomplish the deed, like Elisha, or prayer concerning it, as fellow sufferers,
if you have held back your diligent steps from examining the matter closely with me. Set apart and consecrate your minds to the Lord,
so that through the graciousness of your petition, what pleases our Lord's will may quietly be arranged for my lowly self.
And if it is pleasing [?] to his grace, may he also guide my weakness without disturbance, without stumbling, and without sin,
through the remainder of the life reserved for my frailty in this world, and may I always do, in every action, whatever pleases his will. End.
52. To my kind and honored father, Mar Gabriel, metropolitan bishop, and my dear and beloved brother, Mar Hormizd, bishop.
And if he is aware [?] that the bishop of Beth Lapat wrote to me along with you—he who is still my honored brother, Mar Marammeh. Ishoʿyahb, your brother: greetings in our Lord.
When I encountered the outward form of what you wrote to me, blessed men, I was truly astonished at what had happened.
And because of the haste of the change, I could not even examine them. But when I opened and read the message addressed to me, I was led to even greater astonishment.
First, at this: how that holy man, whom only a little earlier I had asked you to send on my behalf to our common father,
I now find at the head of the ranks of those urging me, at the beginning of the letter—and this although he holds the foremost position among you, that is, among people who know
my quick temper, my stubbornness, and the other troublesome habits of my lack of refinement. Second, on what did your astonishing judgment rely,
that you immediately placed a man whose experience you had not even put to the test at the head of the ranks of the Lord’s forces, before the signal, that is, for peace,
and sent him beyond the [?] borders, as though into the gale called Typhonic Euroclydon?
And third, along with these things: by what compelling force was that humble man overpowered, so that he entered such a storm without hesitation, in faithful obedience?
Although I was greatly astonished at these things, holy fathers, I was also deeply frightened and alarmed. I did not dare to find fault,

but I found it difficult to offer praise. Yet if you say that the recommendation came from me, and that you were encouraged to carry it through because of my confidence, why did you not include me among you, since you trusted me so much?
For I had, just as I still have now, much to show you about his suitability and unsuitability, in matters of which I myself have greater knowledge.
For it is also common knowledge that, in turn, in Assyria and among these neighboring peoples, excellence in admirable conduct,
and a pure mind trained through the study of divine teachings are praised, and a modest appearance adorned with the humility of orderly conduct is honored.
Gentleness, kindness, and humility in judgment are valued. And thanks be to the Lord, who has bestowed these things on this servant of his whom we have mentioned.
But farther away, toward [?], and among people engaged in practical affairs, concerning such things—and among people engaged in practical affairs, concerning, so to speak,
a man [?] and [?] and everything resembling these things. And in these matters, as you yourselves have experienced, perhaps he is lacking,
this man we have mentioned, apart from his lack of practice—or rather, his lack of any encounter with such things.
Unless, however, someone says this: that for the work of God, the work of God itself is sufficient. Yes, I say so too.
But the times also require things suited to the times. Yet if we disregard even this with a faithful mind, everything is possible for the one who believes, as it is written.
Therefore, let the work belong to the Lord. But you, who have been so thoroughly overcome by obedience—did I not instruct you to hold out for a little while without yielding,
and that only until I came? How were you overcome before you even arrived? Rather, I sent you to plead on my behalf, and instructed you to bring our father here.
This was because I was prevented from coming by bonds—that is, by inability—as you yourself also know.
But you forgot the instructions, and not only did you fail to bring our father to me, but you yourself, I think, have also gone far away from me forever.
Not so, blessed one, not so! Instead, be sure to see me, and then go. Take care that you are not disappointed in your hope.
Do not let sorrow over what has happened overcome you. Nor should these reproaches of mine turn you toward discouragement.
Instead, rouse yourself in the hope of our Lord’s help, and ready the shoulder of your obedience for the gentle yoke of Christ.
Now that you have bowed down and taken it up, do not be distressed at carrying it. For, as you read earlier, it is pleasant and light.
And he delights in being perfected in the weak. And if he finds excellence of nature, he makes his work still more beautiful. It is therefore good
that, when you yield to him in both respects, he should carry out through you the work of his church, as he graciously wills.
So that, through the honor and power of the name, your lamp [?] in Elam, and the Lord’s flock may be refreshed by the salt of your kindness. And may
the whole work of your ministry bring praise to the community. May our father’s soul find rest in you, and may he give thanks to our Lord for you.
And you, blessed ones, beloved of my soul, who reproached me about coming—or rather, urged me to come—be convinced and assured that until now opposition has prevailed over my wish.
Now, however, the opposition has diminished a little. Yet I do not find many compelling reasons for my coming there,
especially since I have also heard that our blessed father is preparing to come here. If that happens, then, I ask to see you with him.
But if things turn out otherwise—or rather, if the pressing demands of affairs there cause him to be delayed—keep writing to me as is fitting,
so that, when I find an opportunity to come, I may see you soon. And pray for me, that I may be worthy of God’s mercy and see you in peace.
Up to this point, from his episcopate. From here onward, from his metropolitanate.
